claim: For any unstructured data — speech, images, or text — deep learning is likely going to be the answer for automating and extracting structured information from it.
speaker: Richard Socher
why: Deep learning did become the default method for extracting structure from speech, images and text — Transformer-based ASR, vision models and LLMs displaced feature-engineering pipelines across all three modalities within a few years of this 2015 talk.

claim: PhD programs explicitly titled 'data science' will emerge very soon, following on the heels of new data science master's programs already appearing (e.g., at NYU).
why: Kennesaw State launched what is generally described as the first US PhD explicitly titled Data Science in 2015, two years after this talk, matching the 'very soon' framing.

claim: Multiple universities beyond the first mover will begin offering PhD programs in data science.
why: Many universities followed the first mover — NYU's Center for Data Science PhD opened in Fall 2017 and dozens of data science doctoral programs now exist across the US.

claim: Governments' current insistence on internal/private clouds rather than external cloud infrastructure will eventually change.
speaker: Joe Lonsdale
why: Governments moved decisively onto commercial public cloud — FedRAMP scaled through the 2010s, the CIA's C2S contract went to AWS, and the DoD's $9B JWCC award in 2022 split across AWS, Microsoft, Google and Oracle.

claim: Mass adoption of 'neural software' or a 'neural operating system,' where large language models directly become the running software rather than generating static code, will begin in roughly 10 to 15 years, following the same multi-decade adoption arc as Apple's 'one person, one computer' vision, which took about 50 years from founding to true ubiquity.
speaker: Stephen Balaban

claim: Real enterprise ROI from generative AI is roughly a year away (not multiple years), since most of Mistral's enterprise engagements only recently began the necessary 'building phase' of connecting data and infrastructure, and tooling across the industry remains immature.
speaker: Timothée Lacroix

claim: In the foreseeable future, doctors will increasingly become data scientists themselves, using richer contextual and wearable/behavioral data to make faster, better-supported diagnostic and treatment decisions.
speaker: Ron Gutman
why: Physicians did not become data scientists in any meaningful sense; wearable and behavioral data remained largely outside clinical workflows, and the documented trend over the decade was rising EHR-driven administrative burden and burnout rather than physician-led data analysis.

claim: As patients increasingly demand and pay for immediate, on-demand access to care, insurance payers will eventually pay for that kind of access too.
speaker: Ron Gutman
why: Payers did end up reimbursing on-demand care, but not through the stated mechanism: the driver was the COVID-19 emergency and CMS waivers from 2020, not consumers demanding and paying out of pocket until payers followed, so the trend was right and the causal path was not.

claim: The next five years will be a monumental period of AI adoption growth in healthcare, following a shift from skepticism to serious enterprise buying interest triggered by GPT-4's release.
speaker: Akilesh Bapu

claim: Within 10 years, doing science without using AI models to assist will be considered as unthinkable as being a biologist without a microscope.
speaker: Jeremy Kahn

claim: 2024 will be the year enterprises move generative AI from proof-of-concept into far more production use cases, with some becoming durable, real deployments rather than experiments.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: Some durable enterprise deployments did emerge in 2024, but survey evidence through that year consistently showed the majority of generative AI initiatives still stuck in pilot, with widely reported failure-to-production rates rather than a decisive shift.
timing: Production deployment grew through 2024 but the decisive POC-to-production shift landed later than the stated year.

claim: Enterprises running generative AI applications for more than a year or two will very likely have to switch LLM providers over that time as the technology and vendor landscape evolves.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: Provider switching became routine over 2024-2026 as model leadership changed hands repeatedly and abstraction layers (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Bedrock) were adopted specifically to make swapping providers cheap.

claim: As broader adoption of tools like Textio accelerates how quickly effective job-listing language spreads and saturates, the differentiated advantage of using specific high-performing terminology could get arbitraged away over time.
speaker: Kieran Snyder
why: Whether high-performing job-listing phrasing got arbitraged away by diffusion was never measured publicly; Textio's own effectiveness data is proprietary and no independent study tracks the saturation effect described.

claim: Partner ecosystems will become the most prolific and efficient growth lever businesses can build over the coming decade.
speaker: Bob Moore

claim: In 2026, multi-agent systems will likely become more practically useful, shifting interaction from a single question-and-response model call to a more complex background process involving multiple models that returns a finished artifact.
speaker: Pavel Izmailov

claim: The shortage of data scientists will be solved by a combination of pragmatic, practice-first education and tools that automate the modeling process and automate data science to a degree most people today would consider impossible.
speaker: Jeremy Achin
why: The automation limb largely held — AutoML and later LLM-based tooling automated much of the modeling work to a degree that would have seemed implausible in 2015 — but the shortage limb did not resolve as described: demand grew faster than supply and data/ML roles remained among the hardest to fill through the early 2020s.

claim: Within a few years, essentially every database system and data warehouse will support Arrow-based import and export in some format.
speaker: Wes McKinney
why: Arrow became a genuine industry standard — adopted by Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB, Spark and the ADBC driver ecosystem — but 'essentially every database system and data warehouse' overstates it, since many transactional and legacy systems still have no Arrow path; the verdict hinges on how strictly 'essentially every' is read.

claim: Within five years, more robust abstractions on top of data than plain SQL will emerge, including within the dbt ecosystem itself, as data processing becomes polyglot.
speaker: Tristan Handy

claim: Within five years, the current gap between the modern data stack and machine learning/data science workflows will have been sanded over and will no longer be a salient distinction.
speaker: Tristan Handy

claim: OpenAI aims to have an 'AI intern' capable of autonomously implementing and running week-long engineering/research tasks by the end of next year, contingent on solving long-horizon coherence problems like context compaction and avoiding the model getting stuck in loops.
speaker: Łukasz Kaiser

claim: A purpose-built, clinically aligned AI model optimized for therapeutic goals (intent, alliance, psychological change, behavioral change) can measurably strengthen users' real-world social connections rather than replace them, evidenced by an NYU study showing users gained on average one additional friend or close personal connection after about 10 weeks.
speaker: Daniel
why: The claim rests on an NYU study reported by the speaker that could not be located in public literature; without the study or independent replication the 'one additional close connection after ten weeks' figure cannot be verified, and a vendor-cited result on its own product warrants human review.

claim: The compute cost barrier that currently limits deep learning to well-funded technology companies will fall within a year or two, making it trivially affordable even for hobbyists.
speaker: Hilary Mason
why: The hobbyist limb held — Google Colab's free GPUs (2018) and cheap cloud instances made training and fine-tuning trivially affordable — but the limb implying deep learning would stop being the preserve of well-funded companies failed decisively, as frontier training costs rose into the hundreds of millions.
timing: Hobbyist-affordable deep learning arrived roughly on schedule via free notebook GPUs, but the gap to frontier-scale training widened rather than closed.

claim: As in every industry, the BI market is shifting away from a stack model toward a platform model, in which platform providers ultimately end up winning.
speaker: Anthony Deighton
why: BI consolidated onto platforms owned by large vendors — Salesforce acquired Tableau (2019), Google acquired Looker (2019), and Microsoft Power BI became dominant as part of the broader Microsoft stack, exactly the platform-beats-standalone-stack outcome described.

claim: A principal-level AI engineer, combining current 'L9 with amnesia' code generation ability with a solved contextual memory core, is a tractable near-term goal, likely achievable within a couple of years.
speaker: Misha Laskin

claim: Within about two years, the industry will stop talking about standalone large language models and instead discuss AI systems that orchestrate multiple language models together in more reliable, deterministic ways.
speaker: Ori Goshen
why: By 2025 the industry conversation had shifted from standalone models to compound/agentic systems that orchestrate multiple models with tool use and verification — the Berkeley 'compound AI systems' framing and the agent-framework wave (LangGraph, MCP) landed squarely inside the two-year window.

claim: Over the next six to twelve months, enterprise generative AI adoption will shift from massive experimentation into gradual, then more rigorously measured, production deployment, revealing that some use cases won't be economically viable while others will clearly succeed.
speaker: Ori Goshen
why: The direction was right and economically unviable use cases were indeed culled, but through 2024 enterprises were still overwhelmingly in experimentation, with Gartner projecting 30% of generative AI projects abandoned after proof-of-concept by end of 2025.
timing: The measured-production shift took closer to two years than the stated six to twelve months.

claim: Over the next five to ten years there will be enormous opportunity to build new connected objects differentiated through their apps and services rather than the hardware itself.
why: The value-shift limb held — connected objects did compete on apps and services rather than hardware — but the 'enormous opportunity' limb accrued mainly to incumbent platforms (Amazon, Google, Apple) while the independent connected-device startup cohort largely failed or was acquired cheaply.

claim: The industrial internet will extend the 'software as a service' model to physical machinery — machinery provided as a service, similar to how jet engines are already leased separately from airplanes — at increasingly smaller commercial scales.
why: Equipment-as-a-service did spread beyond jet engines (Rolls-Royce TotalCare, Caterpillar and Hitachi machine leasing with telematics, Philips light-as-a-service), but it stayed a niche commercial model rather than extending broadly to small-scale machinery as predicted.

claim: In-memory analytics is already becoming obsolete, being superseded by 'in-chip' architectures that exploit CPU cache hierarchies directly rather than just moving data from disk to RAM.
speaker: Amit Bendov
why: In-memory analytics did not become obsolete — it remains standard in Spark, DuckDB and cloud warehouses — and no distinct 'in-chip' cache-resident architecture displaced it as a category; cache-aware vectorized execution became an optimization technique inside existing engines, not a successor architecture.

claim: GPUs are set to become a dominant computing force across the analytics stack over the coming decade, the way they already have for machine learning.
speaker: Todd Mostak

claim: Open-source tools like R, rather than traditional commercial analytics platforms like SAS, are becoming the place where the most effective machine learning techniques are developed and adopted.
speaker: Jeremy Howard
why: Open-source decisively became where machine learning is developed — scikit-learn, R, then TensorFlow and PyTorch — while SAS declined into a legacy position and was repeatedly reported to be seeking an exit.

claim: Within five to ten years, the role of data scientist or data engineer will largely disappear or fundamentally change, shifting from manually analyzing spreadsheets toward programming automated systems like Wordsmith.
speaker: Robbie Allen
why: The role did change substantially by 2019-2024 (AutoML, then LLM-assisted analysis, shifted work toward pipeline and system design), but it emphatically did not 'largely disappear' — data engineering became one of the fastest-growing job categories in the period. The disjunctive phrasing 'disappear OR fundamentally change' makes this close to unfalsifiable and is why it needs a human call.

claim: The Bloomberg App Portal will disrupt and democratize financial-services software the way app stores disrupted mobile and video games, letting small, unknown developers compete with large firms and make outsized money and impact.
speaker: Claudio Storelli
why: The Bloomberg App Portal never became an app-store-scale disruption of financial software; no ecosystem of small developers earning outsized returns emerged, and financial-software distribution continued to run through incumbent vendors and direct enterprise sales.

claim: The App Portal could become a precursor to the Bloomberg terminal expanding beyond core financial customers into other verticals, such as media-centric institutions.
speaker: Claudio Storelli
why: The Bloomberg Terminal did not expand into media-centric or other non-financial verticals; it remained a finance-professional product, and Bloomberg's media businesses stayed separate from Terminal distribution.

claim: AI will let accounts-payable software automatically approve routine recurring bills that fall within historical norms, flagging only exceptions and suggesting approval policies, reducing manual review workload over the next year or two.
speaker: Howard Katzenberg
why: AP automation vendors (Glean, Ramp, Bill.com, Coupa) did ship AI-driven anomaly flagging and touchless approval for routine invoices in this window, but the degree to which routine bills are genuinely auto-approved without human review is not publicly measured, so the magnitude of the claim cannot be settled.

claim: Commercial LLM vendor pricing will continue to decline as providers' own compute costs fall and competition increases, so today's LLM API pricing shouldn't be assumed static over the next 12-18 months when deciding whether to build models in-house.
speaker: Howard Katzenberg
why: LLM API pricing fell sharply over the stated window — cost per token for equivalent capability dropped by more than an order of magnitude between 2023 and 2025 across OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, vindicating the advice not to treat pricing as static.

claim: Data-holding companies (like Facebook, telcos, and payment processors) will accrue lasting strategic advantage over algorithm-focused companies, because algorithms will migrate to wherever the proprietary data already lives.
why: Data incumbents did retain advantage in their own domains, but the decade's biggest AI winners (OpenAI, Anthropic) were algorithm-first organizations without proprietary consumer data estates, and algorithms migrated to public web-scale corpora rather than to where private data sat — the stated mechanism largely failed even as the general 'data matters' intuition held.

claim: The role of 'data scientist' will follow the same historical trajectory as 'computer' (once a human job title, now a machine) — roughly five years of human-dominated data science, followed by another five years in which much of that work is automated.
why: The predicted second phase (2017-2022, when 'much of that work is automated' and the human job title fades like the human 'computer') did not occur — data scientist headcount grew sharply through that window and the US BLS ranked it among the fastest-growing occupations, with AutoML supplementing rather than displacing practitioners.

claim: As competitions prove valuable in an industry (e.g., insurance actuarial modeling), competitive pressure among companies in that industry will drive competition prize money to be bid up, as no company wants materially worse models than competitors.
why: No competitive bidding-up of prize money materialized in any industry; Kaggle prize pools plateaued after its 2017 acquisition by Google and the platform's value shifted to talent signalling and community rather than escalating industry-funded purses.

claim: Read-only access to physical systems like connected cars (as with Ford's OpenXC) will soon become common write access, letting apps directly change vehicle behavior (shift points, fuel-air mixture, etc.).
speaker: Jon Bruner
why: Third-party write access to vehicle control never became common — automakers locked down CAN-bus write paths for safety, liability and regulatory reasons, and Ford's OpenXC remained a read-oriented research project rather than a template for app-controlled vehicle behavior.

claim: Big software companies (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Yahoo) will increasingly contribute meaningful machine learning and optimization capability to heavy industry and complex physical systems like passenger airliners in the coming years.
speaker: Jon Bruner
why: Hyperscalers did push ML into heavy industry (Azure and AWS industrial IoT, Google DeepMind's data-centre cooling optimisation, GE-Microsoft partnerships), but aviation and other safety-critical physical systems remained dominated by incumbent suppliers rather than meaningfully reshaped by big software companies.

claim: Location intelligence deserves and will become its own dedicated category in the big data landscape, the same way specialized analytical tools exist for logs and other verticals, since most organizations would benefit substantially from taking advantage of location data.
speaker: Javier de la Torre
why: Location intelligence did become a named analyst category with dedicated vendors (CARTO, Esri, Foursquare/Unfolded, Placer.ai), but it remained a modest specialist segment rather than achieving the standing of a major layer of the data landscape as claimed.

claim: Highly sensitive enterprise data (internal sales figures, employment records) will remain off the public cloud for the near term, but within roughly 10 years, advances in high-security database technology will make cloud storage acceptable even for that data.
why: Within the stated decade highly sensitive enterprise data did move to public cloud — Workday and cloud HR systems hold employment records, Snowflake and BigQuery hold financials, and cloud-native encryption, key management and confidential computing supplied the security advances the claim anticipated.

claim: Within roughly three to four years, sports will be transformed by comprehensive sensor tracking (RFID, etc.) capturing the XYZ position of every player and the ball throughout a game, giving teams a major scouting and play-calling advantage.
why: Comprehensive positional tracking arrived almost exactly on the three-to-four-year schedule: the NBA installed SportVU in all 30 arenas for 2013-14, the NFL rolled out Zebra RFID shoulder-pad tags league-wide by 2015, and MLB launched Statcast in 2015.

claim: Legacy browser market share (IE7/IE8, then ~20% of traffic) will fall to roughly 3-4% within a couple of years, allowing companies to migrate visualization stacks from older libraries like Protovis to modern ones like D3.
why: IE8 alone still held ~16% desktop share in April 2015 per Net Market Share — far above the predicted 3-4% by ~2014 — though the enabling consequence (migration from Protovis to D3) did happen, with D3 becoming the dominant web visualization library.
timing: Legacy-IE share did collapse and D3 did become the standard, but reaching 3-4% took ~4-5 years, not the stated 'couple of years'.

claim: Within 12 months, some real examples will emerge of AI agents acting as full 'micro firms', buying, selling, provisioning infrastructure, and running an entire business end to end on a person's behalf, rather than merely executing individual purchase tasks.
speaker: Emily Sands

claim: It will take roughly one to two years for consumers to build enough trust to delegate major purchasing decisions (like a full back-to-school shopping budget) to an agent entirely, rather than only using AI for product discovery while still personally approving each transaction.
speaker: Emily Sands

claim: Citing industry forecasts, global data volume will grow from about 2.8 zettabytes to 40 zettabytes by 2020, with most of that growth coming from sensors rather than screens/human-generated content.
speaker: Mike Abbott
why: The cited IDC trajectory was met and exceeded — global datasphere reached roughly 64 zettabytes in 2020 against the forecast 40 — and machine/sensor-generated data did become the dominant share of growth.

claim: Within roughly two years, people will feel completely comfortable that all their software can talk to other software in an agentic way, following a similar adoption curve to how REST APIs became ubiquitous two decades ago.
speaker: Aaron Levie

claim: Retail stores will soon have Placemeter-style real-time occupancy/wait information the way New York subway platforms now have countdown-clock signs.
speaker: Alexandre Winter
why: Live store occupancy and wait-time displays did become widespread, but Placemeter itself failed — it was acquired by Netgear in 2016 and shut down — and the capability arrived through Google Popular Times and COVID-era occupancy counters instead.
timing: Real-time occupancy data did become common in retail, but around 2020-21 under pandemic pressure rather than 'soon' after 2013, and not via Placemeter.

claim: Big data is a multi-decade secular trend, not a cyclical fad — it will ultimately underpin every business rather than fading like previous tech hype cycles.
why: The secular-trend limb held — data infrastructure did become foundational to essentially every business — but the specific 'big data' framing did fade as a category exactly the way the claim said it would not, so whether this counts as vindication depends on reading it as being about the substance or the label.

claim: Big data will follow the same multi-decade adoption pattern as previous major technology waves (PCs, cable TV, cell phones) — a long secular trend immune to hype cycles, recessions, and macroeconomic variation, lasting roughly 20 years.

Hadoop will remain the dominant default platform for large-scale data processing but won't replace SQL-based systems — the two paradigms will blend, with SQL-on-Hadoop layers extending Hadoop into workloads it wasn't originally built for.

Several billion-dollar startups will emerge specifically to solve the outstanding problems in big-data infrastructure that Hadoop-based systems haven't cracked: scale, performance, administrative ease, industrial-grade reliability, and security/federation.
why: Multiple billion-dollar companies emerged doing exactly this — Databricks, Snowflake, Confluent, MongoDB and Elastic all built large businesses on the scale, performance, manageability and reliability gaps that Hadoop-era systems left open.

claim: If the EU adopts a unified, low-friction startup legal/tax structure and an internal startup visa, it could become a genuine rival to the US in startups and tech within 20 years; without those reforms, it will remain a relative backwater.

2025 will be the year enterprise generative AI shifts from discrete tasks to full AI-orchestrated workflows, moving beyond productivity gains toward multi-hundred-percent changes in company capacity and capability.
speaker: May Habib
why: The workflow-orchestration limb held — 2025 was widely described as the year enterprise AI moved from discrete tasks to agentic multi-step workflows — but the 'multi-hundred-percent changes in company capacity' limb has no supporting evidence, with measured enterprise productivity gains remaining incremental.

claim: Within three to five years, AI will be sophisticated enough to actually run companies, which is why enterprises are now asking much more sophisticated questions about model training data provenance and governance before buying.
speaker: May Habib

claim: The Internet of Things will really be won on services layered on top of connected hardware rather than the hardware itself, since the physical things are meaningless unless connected into interesting service experiences.
speaker: Peter Semmelhack
why: IoT value did accrue to the service layer — Ring, Nest and Tesla monetise subscriptions and OTA software while the hardware became commoditised, and hardware-only IoT startups largely failed.

claim: Makers of physical products that go online will increasingly need to treat developers as a second customer alongside end users, fundamentally changing product design.
speaker: Peter Semmelhack
why: Some connected-product makers did build developer surfaces (Matter, SmartThings, Tesla's API ecosystem), but the dominant pattern went the other way — Nest curtailed its developer API in 2019 and most consumer IoT vendors closed rather than opened their platforms.

claim: AI will disproportionately amplify already-above-average professionals (developers, lawyers, VCs, doctors) into 'super-superhumans,' while automating away average-performer roles, plausibly reducing total jobs even as it unlocks new creative capability for everyone.
speaker: Amr Awadallah

claim: Hadoop's parallel execution layer, having already expanded from MapReduce-only to include engines like Impala, will continue diversifying with many more execution frameworks to come.
speaker: Jeff Hammerbacher
why: The execution layer diversified exactly as described — Spark, Tez, Flink, Presto and Impala all became first-class engines over YARN/HDFS, ending MapReduce's monopoly on the platform.

claim: Research on fair, accountable, and transparent algorithms will become standard commercial practice rather than staying purely academic, as users become more educated about how data products affect their lives.
speaker: Solmaz Shahalizadeh
why: Fairness and transparency work did move into commercial practice via the EU AI Act (2024), model cards and enterprise AI-governance tooling, but calling it 'standard' overstates the outcome — several major responsible-AI teams were cut in the 2023 layoffs even as regulation advanced.

claim: The industry framing will shift away from 'human versus AI' toward 'human with AI,' with more tools built specifically to combine human and artificial intelligence rather than treating them as competing.
speaker: Solmaz Shahalizadeh
why: The 'human with AI' framing became the industry default — the entire copilot/assistant product category launched on exactly that positioning, displacing the replacement framing common in 2019.

claim: Causal inference (as distinct from the current machine learning hype) will see renewed investment and solve many practical business-analytics problems that pure ML approaches currently struggle to answer.
speaker: Solmaz Shahalizadeh
why: Causal tooling did mature and get commercial investment (DoWhy, EconML, uplift modelling in marketing and experimentation platforms), but it did not become the answer to business analytics problems in the way described — attention and budget went overwhelmingly to generative AI instead.

claim: Enterprise voice data will hit a tipping point where every voice interaction inside a business becomes easily accessible via API, as infrastructure vendors like Cisco and Avaya open up their data to increase the value of their own platforms.
speaker: Evan Macmillan
why: Voice data did become far more API-accessible via cloud contact centres (Amazon Connect in 2017, Twilio, Genesys Cloud), but this came from new cloud entrants rather than Cisco and Avaya opening their platforms as the mechanism predicted, and 'every voice interaction inside a business' remains far from reality.

claim: Machine translation quality will improve roughly 10x within a few years, acting as a force multiplier for synthetic video content creation across languages.
speaker: Victor Riparbelli and Matthias Niessner
why: Translation quality did improve substantially as LLMs displaced dedicated MT systems, but '10x' has no defined metric — BLEU and human-preference scores are not on a common scale — so whether the stated magnitude was met cannot be settled objectively.

claim: Within three to five years, video/image generation technology will progress to enabling full narrative content (e.g. a full movie) to be generated automatically from text like a book.
speaker: Victor Riparbelli and Matthias Niessner
why: Sora (2024) and Veo (2025) delivered dramatic text-to-video progress and AI-assisted short films became common, but generating a coherent full-length narrative feature automatically from a text source remains unachieved, so the specific end-state described was not reached in three to five years.
timing: Generation quality advanced enormously inside the window, but automatic full-length narrative from a book has not arrived by 2026.

claim: Doctors will not meaningfully change their data-entry behavior on any timeframe that matters for a startup — realistically not for another 10-15 years — because EMRs (including Flatiron's own) are built for physician workflow and billing, not population health or informatics.
speaker: Zach Weinberg

claim: The share of US oncology providers addressable by Flatiron's combined EHR and analytics products, currently about 90%, will reach 100% within two years.
speaker: Zach Weinberg
why: Flatiron Health's internal addressable-provider percentage was never published, and Roche acquired the company for $1.9B in 2018, so the 90%-to-100% figure cannot be checked against any public source.

claim: The traditional enterprise software model (a team builds software, hands it to a direct sales force, sells license-only at ~80% margins) is going away — being eaten from below by bottoms-up/product-led adoption and from above by services-heavy go-to-market.
speaker: Martin Casado
why: Both pressures materialised as described — product-led growth became the default motion for developer and SaaS tooling, while AI-era enterprise deals increasingly carry heavy forward-deployed-engineering and services components that compress the classic 80%-margin license model.

claim: It will take roughly 5-7 years before big data analytics tools become accessible enough that non-programmers, not just people who know Python or R, can independently extract insight from data.
why: Self-service BI (Tableau, Power BI) partly delivered this inside the window for dashboarding, but open-ended insight extraction without code only became real once natural-language data interfaces arrived with LLMs well after the predicted 2017-2019 date.
timing: Genuine non-programmer independent analysis arrived with LLM interfaces around 2023-24, roughly a decade out rather than the stated 5-7 years.

claim: Software will increasingly take the form of 'intelligent agents' that interpret data and make or suggest decisions on a human's behalf, extending closed-feedback-loop personalization systems already used for content recommendation.
why: Software did take exactly this form — the agent category emerged as predicted, with systems that interpret data and take or recommend actions on a user's behalf becoming a central product paradigm by the mid-2020s.

claim: The field will increasingly adopt hybrid AI approaches combining deep learning with classical, symbolic AI techniques, without necessarily branding them as 'hybrid' — similar to how IBM quietly rebranded unrelated internal projects under the 'Watson' name after its Jeopardy fame.
speaker: Gary Marcus
why: Modern systems do combine neural models with symbolic components — tool use, code execution, retrieval, formal verifiers like Lean in the Erdos work — which Marcus reads as vindication, but the field attributes the gains to scaling and RL rather than to a symbolic turn, so whether this counts as the predicted hybrid adoption is genuinely contested.

claim: By 2030 there will be five billion middle-class people globally, at least half of whom will be knowledge workers expecting information at the speed of thought.
speaker: Prakash Nanduri

claim: Natural language processing will be the next major field to be transformed by deep learning, following speech recognition and image recognition.
speaker: Yann LeCun
why: NLP was indeed the next field transformed, and decisively so — the Transformer (2017), BERT (2018) and the GPT line remade language processing exactly in the sequence after speech and vision that LeCun described.

claim: The window of opportunity for startups to compete purely on deep learning expertise is closing quickly, as the pool of trained practitioners grows and gets absorbed by large tech companies or acquired startups.
speaker: Yann LeCun
why: The window did close for the 2014-era deep-learning acquihire wave as talent was absorbed, but it reopened spectacularly a few years later — OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral and others were founded and reached enormous scale on exactly the model-expertise-as-differentiator thesis LeCun said was closing.

claim: Building machines more intelligent than humans ('superintelligence') is a very long way off, since basic scientific principles like effective unsupervised learning remain unsolved, contrary to near-term existential-risk framings.
speaker: Yann LeCun
why: The conclusion limb still holds — superhuman general intelligence has not arrived — but the stated premise limb failed: self-supervised learning on unlabelled data turned out to be exactly what powered the LLM era, so the scientific obstacle LeCun named was substantially overcome.

claim: Self-driving trucks will operate on freeways within the next 18 months, ahead of self-driving passenger taxis, because moving goods has clearer economic value and avoids the hardest urban driving problems.
speaker: Mike Volpi
why: Both limbs failed: TuSimple's first fully driverless highway run came in December 2021, past the stated window, and driverless robotaxis actually arrived first (Waymo opened fully driverless public rides in Phoenix in October 2020), reversing the predicted ordering; Waymo then shut its trucking program in 2023.
timing: A driver-out highway run did happen, but in December 2021 — roughly a year past the 18-month window — and commercial scale never followed.

claim: Deriving competitive advantage from business data insights, rather than physical scale, will be the single most important enterprise investment theme over the next decade, with most companies still clueless on how to do it.
speaker: Mike Volpi

claim: AI adoption is at an inflection point analogous to the 'big data' wave of six or seven years earlier, and will follow a similar trajectory as companies find it increasingly hard to ignore.
speaker: Dan Scholnick
why: AI followed the big-data adoption arc closely, including the hype peak and the enterprise scramble not to be left behind, with 2016 proving to be an accurate inflection call ahead of the 2017-2019 ML platform wave and the later generative surge.

claim: As a self-described singularitarian, Dan believes everything will eventually be automatable, expecting this within the next 20 years rather than 50.
speaker: Dan Scholnick

claim: For the next five to ten years, machine learning systems will still require heavy human involvement to generate training data and handle the share of model outputs that fall short of accuracy thresholds.
speaker: Dan Scholnick
why: Heavy human involvement remained essential throughout the window — RLHF made human preference labelling central to frontier training and the data-labelling industry grew rather than shrank, with Meta paying roughly $14B for a stake in Scale AI in 2025.

claim: Human-level general intelligence will not be achieved in the next decade, and likely not within the next two or three decades either.
speaker: Jerome Pesenti

claim: The roughly 10x-per-year growth rate in AI model compute/size is unsustainable and will hit a wall or diminishing returns, forcing a shift toward efficiency and hardware-driven gains.
speaker: Jerome Pesenti
why: The 10x-per-year trajectory did break down and the field pivoted hard to efficiency — mixture-of-experts, distillation, quantisation and inference-time compute became the main levers, alongside hardware gains, rather than continued brute-force parameter growth.

claim: Hiring, talent management, and workforce planning will shift away from relying on branded higher-education credentials toward technology-specific skill credentials that directly measure what someone actually knows.
speaker: Aaron Skonnard
why: Skills-based hiring did gain real ground — major employers and several US states dropped degree requirements and vendor certifications proliferated — but branded higher-education credentials remain the dominant screen, so the shift was partial rather than the reorientation described.

claim: 2024 will be the year of 'generative feedback loops,' where generative models write corrected or new data back into vector databases as embeddings, marking a seismic, bidirectional shift in how models and databases interact.
speaker: Bob van Luijt
why: 'Generative feedback loops' did not become a defining theme of 2024 or enter general usage; the year's actual vector-database story was consolidation and the absorption of vector search into general-purpose databases like Postgres via pgvector.

claim: The crowd-labor platform layer won't mature to the point of true self-service (build-and-sell-with-a-credit-card) within a few months — existing applications will remain vertically integrated with their platforms for a while longer.
speaker: Joseph Turian
why: The crowd-labor layer did not reach credit-card self-service within a few months, and vertically integrated data-labelling businesses like Scale AI and Appen remained the dominant model for years afterward.

claim: The traditional business process outsourcing (BPO) market will shrink as enterprises redirect spending toward crowd labor for the same categories of tasks.
speaker: Joseph Turian
why: BPO did not shrink — the global market continued growing through the 2010s and 2020s, and the genuine threat to it emerged much later from generative AI rather than from the crowd-labor substitution the claim described.

claim: Within the next five to ten years, AI/machine learning will become universally mainstream across companies, with most having hundreds or thousands of automated systems handling ordering, cash management, customer targeting, and similar processes.
speaker: Florian Douetteau

claim: BI tools that natively query JSON/document data will eventually emerge, but it's a genuinely hard UI problem and won't happen soon — it's a long-term development, not something arriving imminently.
speaker: Eliot Horowitz
why: The prediction that native JSON BI would come only slowly proved accurate — mature document-aware analytics arrived years later through engines like DuckDB and Snowflake's semi-structured support rather than through any near-term BI breakthrough.

claim: Within 5-10 years, developers will settle on a small toolbox of database types (roughly three general-purpose options, plus a few niche ones) rather than either a single one-size-fits-all database or a dozen fragmented options.
speaker: Dwight Merriman
why: Consolidation toward a small default set did occur (Postgres in particular absorbed enormous share, alongside MySQL and MongoDB), but the ecosystem simultaneously fragmented with a new wave of specialized engines (vector, time-series, OLAP), so whether developers 'settled on roughly three' depends entirely on where you draw the general-purpose/niche line.

claim: Among NoSQL data models (key-value, big-table-style, document, graph), the JSON document-oriented model will emerge as the standard most of the ecosystem converges on.
speaker: Dwight Merriman
why: The JSON document model did become the ecosystem default — MongoDB's model won the NoSQL category outright and JSON support became mandatory even in relational systems, with Postgres JSONB now a standard tool.

claim: An entire ecosystem of adjacent tools (analytics, presentation, messaging/web-services technologies built on formats like BSON) will grow up around NoSQL databases, creating opportunities beyond the databases themselves.
speaker: Dwight Merriman
why: A substantial adjacent ecosystem did grow up around document databases — Atlas and its BI/charts tooling, Realm sync, plus an independent layer of connectors and analytics integrations built on the document/BSON model.

claim: Turning free text and prose into fully trustworthy structured data via NLP remains at a very early stage, with a long road still ahead despite continued community progress.
speaker: Joe Hellerstein
why: The assessment was accurate for years afterward — reliable text-to-structured-data extraction stayed unsolved through the late 2010s, and even current LLM extraction requires verification layers because of hallucination, confirming the 'long road' framing.

claim: As more people have unbelievable experiences with AI customer service, they will increasingly expect and demand to interact with AI over phone, SMS, and email, and that will become the norm within the next few years.
speaker: Mike Murchison

claim: The AI industry as a whole will exceed $100 billion in revenue by the end of this year, up from roughly sub-$1 billion in 2023, driven by usage growth at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's Gemini/Vertex products, though China's comparable figure will likely be roughly 10x smaller due to less pervasive domestic AI adoption.
speaker: Dylan Patel

claim: AI systems will become both more capable and more secure over the next two years, but the central challenge is whether safety work keeps pace with the rapidly expanding 'control surface' (autonomy, integration, actuation) of deployed AI, not whether safety improves at all.
speaker: Zico Kolter

claim: ZestFinance's machine-learning underwriting technique will work across the entire lending industry, across all consumer segments and all lending products.
speaker: Shawn Budde
why: ZestFinance's approach did not generalise across the whole lending industry and all products; the company retreated from direct lending, rebranded to Zest AI and narrowed to selling underwriting software mainly to credit unions and auto lenders.

claim: Widespread adoption of this technique is worth about $20 billion a year in lower credit losses, which will lower what consumers pay for credit and expand credit availability.
speaker: Shawn Budde
why: The $20 billion annual credit-loss reduction figure was a vendor projection contingent on industry-wide adoption that never occurred, and no public measurement of realised savings from ML underwriting exists at that scope.

claim: The ability of AI models to solve complex problems by planning and using tools will change what it means to do most jobs within the next couple of years.
speaker: Jonathan Rosenbluth

claim: Fully replicating human social/behavioral reasoning from first principles (rather than using human-judgment training data) is roughly 30-50 years away and effectively equivalent to building general AI.
speaker: Sam Anthony

claim: Data discovery tools capable of spreadsheet-like ease at unlimited scale will eventually take over and replace the traditional data warehouse stack entirely, within the next few decades.
speaker: Sandy Steier

claim: Data will keep arriving roughly 60% faster year over year, meaning about 10x more data volume and potentially 20-100x more required processing power within five years, which will break existing infrastructure approaches on cost or performance.
speaker: Vid Jain
why: The data-growth limb was roughly right — global data volume grew about an order of magnitude over the window — but the consequence limb failed: cloud object storage and elastic compute absorbed the growth economically instead of existing infrastructure approaches breaking on cost or performance.

claim: Python will overtake Java as the dominant language for building data applications within the next year.
speaker: Vid Jain
why: Python passed Java on GitHub's Octoverse in 2019 and on TIOBE only in late 2020 — two to three years after the predicted one-year window — though for data work specifically Python's lead was already established earlier, which is what makes this partial rather than simply wrong.
timing: Python did overtake Java, but the crossover landed 2019-2020 depending on the index, not within the stated one year.

claim: Given current techniques, compute, and the right feedback loops, the AI industry is on track within the next two to three years to build something at least as capable as most humans at most computer-facing tasks, a working definition of AGI.
speaker: Sholto Douglas

claim: The single most actionable piece of advice for individuals is to plan for a world where personal leverage increases dramatically, since within a year or two people will be able to manage a team of AI agents working around the clock on their behalf.
speaker: Sholto Douglas

claim: The modern data stack sector will likely see continued consolidation, with larger platforms like Databricks, Snowflake, dbt, or Fivetran growing bigger by adding functionality and acquiring smaller struggling startups in 2024-2025 and beyond.
why: Consolidation played out exactly as named — Fivetran acquired Census and Tobiko Data, then merged with dbt Labs in a deal announced October 2025 and completed June 2026, while Databricks absorbed Tabular and Neon.

claim: Complete perfection in AI video generation, where there is absolutely no way to tell it's generated, is still a couple of years away, especially for complex a-roll (talking) footage where core problems remain unsolved.
speaker: Gaurav Misra

claim: The current need to manually define and orchestrate specialized sub-agents (each with narrow roles and tools) will likely become unnecessary within 6-12 months, as models improve enough to handle large context and many tools without getting overloaded.
speaker: Boris Cherny

claim: SaaS is entering a 'Cambrian explosion,' producing many more new categories and species of company rather than simply migrating a fixed set of legacy enterprise software categories to the cloud.
speaker: Sarah Guo
why: SaaS did produce genuinely new categories rather than merely porting legacy ones — data observability, vector databases, AI evaluation, LLM gateways and agent infrastructure all emerged as venture-scale segments with no on-premise predecessor.

claim: Security spending will continue shifting from legacy on-premise tooling toward re-architected cloud/multi-cloud and zero-trust approaches, with the software portion of the security market growing faster than the services portion, as internet-tied commerce and data value keep growing.
speaker: Sarah Guo
why: Security spend shifted decisively to cloud-native and zero-trust architectures, and the software side outgrew services — validated by the scale of cloud-security outcomes such as Google's roughly $32B agreement to acquire Wiz in 2025.

claim: Data privacy and residency regulation (GDPR, CCPA, and successors) will continue moving in the direction of requiring companies to know much more about their own data and have better, more distributed architectural controls, which most companies are currently unprepared for.
speaker: Sarah Guo
why: Privacy regulation expanded exactly along the predicted axis — a dozen-plus US state privacy laws followed CCPA, the EU AI Act added data-governance duties in 2024, and data-residency requirements drove sovereign-cloud regions from every hyperscaler.

claim: Within two to five years, the main problem with enterprise AI agents won't be model quality or relevance, since models will keep improving, but boring operational issues like stale RAG data, security leaks, and understanding which users are driving disproportionate cost.
speaker: Florian Douetteau

claim: If AI model capability were frozen today, enterprises could fully diffuse and implement it within 2-3 years, but because breakthroughs keep arriving faster than customers can implement stable architectures (and each breakthrough often obsoletes the prior implementation), actual enterprise-wide agentic diffusion will take on the order of a decade or more, with no clear 'end state.'
speaker: Aaron Levie

claim: Enterprise software companies will converge on a dual business model within about three years: a seat-based model for human end users and a consumption-based model for agent-driven usage, with the relative size of each varying by category, but full transition to pure headless/consumption pricing is unlikely since GUI-based interaction remains genuinely useful for many tasks.
speaker: Aaron Levie

claim: With about 87 million US knowledge workers scheduling roughly 10 billion formal meetings a year, this is a problem that can only be solved through machine automation, not by scaling human assistants.
speaker: Dennis Mortensen & Marcos Jimenez
why: Scheduling did get automated, but not by the standalone AI-assistant model the claim implied — x.ai itself failed and sold its assets to Bizzabo in 2021, with the problem absorbed instead by Calendly-style self-service booking and calendar features.

claim: Big tech collectively will execute on the vision of language models plus scaffolding to build 95-98% of what's achievable within current physical power and compute constraints over the next two to five years, transforming society dramatically by 2030, even though this shouldn't be conflated with a sudden discontinuity or singularity.
speaker: Nathan Lambert and Luca

claim: Over time, most companies will begin using public clouds for a significant part of what they do, with the data warehouse being an important part of that shift.
speaker: Bob Muglia
why: Public cloud became the default for most enterprise workloads and the cloud data warehouse was indeed central to that shift — Snowflake itself reached a $70B+ IPO in 2020 on precisely this thesis, alongside BigQuery and Redshift.

claim: Forrester projected that over 25% of enterprises would be using graph databases in production by 2017.
speaker: Emil Eifrem
why: The cited Forrester projection of >25% enterprise graph-database production use by 2017 was not met — Gartner still put graph technology at roughly 10% of data and analytics innovations as of 2021, four years past the deadline.

claim: Graph databases will continue spreading vertical by vertical across industries, as they already have in software, financial services, telecom, logistics, and retail, in the same way software has been described as 'eating the world.'
speaker: Emil Eifrem
why: Graph did spread into more verticals (fraud, supply chain, knowledge graphs, and later GraphRAG), but nothing like a software-eating-the-world trajectory materialised — Gartner still measured graph at roughly 10% of data and analytics innovations in 2021, six years on.

claim: Streaming technology will remain a fairly niche technology among existing batch systems until its tooling ecosystem (like dbt for batch SQL) reaches the same maturity level batch tooling has today.
speaker: Arjun Narayan
why: Streaming did remain the niche relative to batch through the window, and the diagnosis was borne out by the tooling gap the industry then tried to close — dbt only shipped streaming-oriented support later and Materialize itself repositioned around operational use cases.

claim: Real-time, freely navigable AI-generated worlds and video generation (analogous to real-time conversation with a language model) are technologically already achievable today and will become a major industry focus over the coming months, unlocking new use cases beyond anything seen before.
speaker: Chris Valenzuela
why: Navigable generative world models did become a significant industry thread — Google's Genie 3 and comparable real-time world-model work landed in 2025 — but adoption was research-and-demo scale rather than the broad unlocking of new use cases described.
timing: Real-time interactive world models did become a major focus, but over roughly a year rather than 'the coming months'.

claim: Police departments broadly are becoming ready to move their data to the cloud, following early movers like on-officer body camera video storage.
speaker: Scott Crouch and EJ Bensing
why: Law enforcement did move to cloud at scale, led by body-camera video as predicted — Axon's Evidence.com became the dominant cloud evidence platform and CJIS-compliant government cloud regions made cloud adoption standard for police IT.

claim: Within two to three years, everyone will be using something like Granola, since AI-powered contextual workspaces will become as fundamental to work as note-taking itself, regardless of which specific company builds the winning product.
speaker: Chris Pedregal

claim: Big-data-driven decisioning capabilities that look speculative or impossible today will become operational reality within about two to three years.
speaker: Arnab Gupta
why: By 2015-2016 the seemingly-impossible decisioning capabilities were still mostly confined to large tech and financial firms; broad operational reality for automated decisioning arrived with the ML platform and later LLM waves well after the stated window.
timing: Advanced automated decisioning did become operational, but over roughly a decade rather than the stated two to three years.

claim: Meaningful cross-industry exposure and adoption of these analytics techniques (beyond early-adopter verticals like financial services) won't be visible until around 2014-2015.
speaker: Arnab Gupta
why: The cautious timing call was accurate — cross-industry adoption beyond financial services did become visible around 2014-2015 as retail, telco and healthcare analytics programmes scaled, matching the stated lag rather than the immediate uptake others predicted.

claim: LLM hallucination won't be fully solved for roughly five years, and will unlock industries sequentially, with regulated industries like healthcare and finance being the last to adopt LLMs in production because their outputs must be auditable.
speaker: William Falcon

claim: The global data visualization tools market will reach almost $20 billion by 2031.
speaker: Pamela Thomas and Emma Cramer

claim: As the open, standardized lakehouse ecosystem matures, enterprises will no longer need the proprietary data warehouse systems that have existed since the 1980s.
speaker: Ali Ghodsi
why: Open table formats did become the standard substrate — Iceberg won broad adoption and even Snowflake embraced it — but enterprises plainly still need and buy proprietary warehouses, with Snowflake growing throughout, so the stronger 'no longer need' claim failed even as the architectural direction held.

claim: The volume of public data available through platforms like Enigma will grow substantially beyond current levels in the coming months and years as government open-data mandates expand from federal agencies to contractors and state/local agencies.
speaker: Jeremy Bronfman
why: Public data volumes did grow and the OPEN Government Data Act (2019) mandated machine-readable federal data, but the expansion to contractors and state/local agencies was uneven, and Enigma itself abandoned the public-data-platform business to pivot to SMB intelligence.

claim: Tooling for ML/AI pipelines will 'go wide and deep': more large-scale platform tools for designing entire pipelines, plus deeper point solutions at each pipeline stage (experiment management, model profiling, model compilation).
speaker: Dillon Erb
why: MLOps went both wide and deep exactly as described — end-to-end platforms (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Databricks ML) alongside deep point tools for experiment tracking (Weights & Biases), model profiling and compilation (ONNX, TVM).

claim: The boundary between edge and data-center deployment will merge, and specific hardware targets will become almost entirely abstracted away by ML deployment platforms.
speaker: Dillon Erb
why: The abstraction limb partly held — ONNX, TVM and managed deployment platforms did hide many hardware targets — but the edge/data-centre boundary did not merge; if anything it hardened, as frontier inference concentrated in large GPU data centres while edge deployment remained a distinct discipline.

claim: Continual learning is unlikely to see a genuine efficiency breakthrough in 2026 despite being a hot topic at NeurIPS, given catastrophic forgetting risks and the practical danger of updating a live, expensive, hosted model; a real breakthrough is more plausibly a 2027 development, offered as a low-confidence prediction.
speaker: Sebastian Raschka

claim: As Hadoop-ecosystem platforms become more productized, IT consulting around implementing them will decline over time, even as demand for data-science consulting stays high.
why: Hadoop implementation consulting did collapse as managed cloud services productised the stack — the Cloudera-Hortonworks merger in 2019 marked the end of that services market — while demand for data-science and later AI consulting kept growing.

claim: People who combine data/technical skill with business judgment (data scientists) will become the most important people in business, and hiring will shift toward that hybrid profile even for traditionally non-technical roles.
why: The hiring-shift limb held — data literacy became an expectation across non-technical roles and analytics skills spread into marketing, finance and operations — but the 'most important people in business' limb overshot, as data scientists were among the roles hit by the 2022-2024 tech layoffs rather than ascending to primacy.

claim: Physical keyboards for programming won't disappear for a long time, since it's hard to imagine anything doing a meaningfully better job outside of a general AI that's better at programming than humans are.
speaker: Ben Medlock
why: Physical keyboards remain the primary programming interface a decade later; even with LLM coding assistants and voice input available, typed text stayed the dominant modality exactly as predicted.

claim: AI agents will contribute more to GDP than human workers within a decade, but adoption will be heavily backloaded, and organizations will still be deploying AI in its current chatbot form in ten years, similar to how some businesses still only accept cash.
speaker: George Sivulka

claim: The 'big data' terminology will shift and the tools needed to work with data at that scale will become commoditized.
speaker: Hilary Mason
why: Both parts came true — the 'big data' label faded from usage, and the tooling commoditised to the point that a laptop running DuckDB or a cheap cloud warehouse handles what once required a Hadoop cluster.

claim: Over the next five to ten years, enterprise data architecture will shift from the traditional data warehouse to a Hadoop-centric 'data reservoir' model where data lands without upfront schema decisions and structure emerges through usage.
speaker: Ben Werther
why: The schema-on-read data-lake architecture limb was correct and became dominant, but the Hadoop-centric mechanism limb failed completely — the winning substrate was cloud object storage with lakehouse table formats, and Platfora itself was absorbed by Workday in 2016.

claim: A whole ecosystem of tools and companies will build up around the 'data reservoir' architectural model.
speaker: Ben Werther
why: A large ecosystem did grow around the schema-on-read lake model — catalogs, table formats, query engines and governance tools (Iceberg, Delta, Trino, Unity Catalog, Databricks) constitute exactly the tooling layer predicted, even though the 'data reservoir' term itself did not survive.

claim: Predictive modeling techniques used for legislative outcomes will extend to legal proceedings, producing something like 'high frequency litigation' — predicting trial or case outcomes the way FiscalNote predicts bill passage.
speaker: Tim Hwang & Vlad
why: Litigation outcome prediction did become a real commercial category (Lex Machina, Premonition, and later LLM-based legal analytics), but nothing resembling the high-frequency-trading analogy emerged, and several US federal courts restrict judge-level outcome analytics.

claim: Within three years, most enterprises and organizations will have brought language models into meaningful use in customer service, sales, operations, back-office, legal, and often their core product experience.
speaker: Jeff Huber
why: By 2026 language models were in meaningful production use across customer service, sales, back-office and legal functions at most large enterprises, and embedded in core product experiences — surveys through 2025-26 consistently showed majority enterprise adoption in at least one such function.

claim: Companies without a plan to build a single view of the customer will be at a serious strategic disadvantage against internet-era companies (like Google, Facebook, and Amazon) that already have and act on that unified customer record.
speaker: Peter Reinhardt
why: The customer-data-platform category did become mainstream (Segment sold to Twilio for $3.2B in 2020), but the predicted competitive penalty is not evident — plenty of companies without unified customer records continued to do well, and privacy rules like ATT cut the other way.

claim: The private markets space will eventually have its own 'Yahoo Finance' and its own 'Bloomberg,' and CB Insights intends to become that space's Bloomberg.
speaker: Anand Sanwal
why: The category limb held — private-market data platforms (CB Insights, PitchBook, Crunchbase) did become the Yahoo-Finance-equivalent layer — but the specific ambition limb did not: PitchBook, under Morningstar, rather than CB Insights, became the closest thing to the space's Bloomberg.

claim: Widespread adoption of connected-device technologies like SmartThings could eliminate around 19% of carbon emissions through basic energy-efficiency use cases (like automatically turning things off when people leave).
speaker: Alex Hawkinson
why: Smart-home adoption delivered nothing close to a 19% emissions reduction; global emissions continued rising through the decade and the measured savings from consumer connected-device energy management are a rounding error against that figure.

claim: Big-data machine learning techniques will take hold in financial services credit underwriting much faster than FICO's roughly 30-year path to mainstream adoption, though still likely a matter of years rather than becoming immediately common.
why: The calibrated middle position proved right — ML underwriting did move much faster than FICO's 30-year arc, with regulators issuing explicit guidance on AI credit models by the early 2020s, while still taking the several years the claim allowed rather than becoming immediately common.

claim: Other lenders will eventually adopt machine-learning-based underwriting techniques similar to ZestFinance's, within a couple of years to a decade.
why: Within the stated couple-of-years-to-a-decade window, ML-based underwriting did become widespread — Upstart built a public company on it, incumbent lenders adopted comparable models, and Zest AI sold the technique to credit unions and banks.

claim: Models currently too large to run on mobile devices will run on mobile within the next year.
speaker: Antoine Bordes
why: Within roughly a year, on-device inference for previously server-only models became routine — Apple shipped Core ML in June 2017 and Google published MobileNets in April 2017, both explicitly aimed at running large vision models on phones.

claim: The reinforcement-learning environments used to train AI models, currently fairly simple, will become significantly more complex and diverse over the next few years, which is the key mechanism by which AI will generalize beyond verifiable domains like coding and math into more ambiguous fields like law and consulting.
speaker: Bryan Catanzaro

claim: Voice-controllable devices will grow from current levels to between 2 and 3 billion by 2021, a faster growth trajectory than smartphones experienced after their introduction.
speaker: Rand Hindi
why: Counting devices with an assistant available, the 2-3 billion figure was met or exceeded by 2021 (Google Assistant alone claimed 1B devices in 2019, Siri 500M+, plus Alexa and Bixby), but headline counts vary by several billion depending on whether the metric is devices shipped-with-capability or active users — the verdict flips on that choice.

claim: As driverless cars and IoT devices become ubiquitous and networked, there will be a genuine scaling problem where the technology becomes risky, such as multi-car pileups from hacking or software bugs.
speaker: Gary Marcus
why: The IoT-scale risk limb was borne out — Mirai-class botnets and infrastructure attacks like Colonial Pipeline showed exactly the networked fragility described — but the specific driverless-car limb did not, because autonomous vehicles never reached the ubiquity needed for multi-car pileups from software faults.

claim: AI will keep improving gradually rather than arriving in one dramatic 'Singularity' moment, so society should start planning for its risks well before that.
speaker: Gary Marcus
why: AI progress since 2016 has been rapid but incremental and continuous rather than a discontinuous takeoff, and the advance planning Marcus urged did materialise through the EU AI Act, the US executive order and the AI-safety-institute network.

claim: The billions of location-emitting mobile devices worldwide will become the key infrastructure for delivering contextually relevant services broadly, beyond just Foursquare.
speaker: Blake Shaw
why: Mobile location signals did become general infrastructure for contextual services well beyond Foursquare — powering Google Maps popular times, delivery and rideshare logistics, retail footfall analytics and a location-data industry that Foursquare itself pivoted to serve.

claim: Within five to ten years, people will stop consuming ten blue links and instead interact with a chatbot/assistant the way they'd ask another person, and Google won't hold a single monopoly in that interface era since it's already behind.
speaker: Aravind Srinivas

claim: 2024 will be the year of AI adoption industry-wide, with even traditionally cautious sectors like banking, government, and healthcare forced to start adopting generative AI as its capabilities become undeniable.
speaker: Des Traynor
why: 2024 saw broad experimentation and genuine movement in banking, but government and healthcare adoption lagged within that year, and Gartner's finding that a large share of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof-of-concept undercuts the 'year of adoption' framing.
timing: Adoption in the cautious regulated sectors accelerated mainly in 2025-26 rather than within 2024.

claim: Fundamental alternative computing paradigms like quantum, neuromorphic, and optical computing remain roughly 15 years out from practical production relevance.
speaker: Michael James

claim: The virtual machine, the technical foundation DigitalOcean was built on, will continue to phase out in favor of containerized applications and eventually serverless/functions, with cloud providers facing a hard multi-tenancy challenge as this transition accelerates.
speaker: Ben Uretsky
why: The containerisation limb held decisively — Kubernetes became the default deployment substrate — but the VM did not phase out; it persists as the isolation primitive underneath containers and returned to prominence as microVMs (Firecracker) for exactly the multi-tenancy problem the claim identified.

claim: Over at least the next 10 years, companies will increasingly need databases that solve for horizontal scale, survivability, wide-area consistency, and complexity as they become more global and mobile.
speaker: Spencer Kimball
why: Distributed SQL became a real and growing category over the stated decade — CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB and TiDB all built substantial businesses on horizontal scale with survivability and wide-area consistency.

claim: As official government economic data releases become delayed or unreliable (e.g. during a government shutdown), synthetic/substitute data sources (like ADP's employment estimates) will likely see wider adoption once early users demonstrate their value, eventually becoming broadly used rather than a narrow informational edge.
speaker: Matt Ober
why: Alternative and private data sources did move from niche edge to broad use — the alt-data industry institutionalised through the 2020s, and reliance on private substitutes grew further as federal statistical releases faced disruption and reduced sample quality.

claim: B2B marketing and sales interactions will increasingly be automated end-to-end, with predictive data driving the right message, channel, and timing rather than humans manually orchestrating each touchpoint.
speaker: Amanda Kahlow
why: B2B go-to-market did become substantially automated and predictive-data-driven — intent data, ABM orchestration and AI-driven sequencing became standard, and 6sense itself grew to a multi-billion-dollar valuation on that thesis.

claim: Non-human traffic will soon dominate the internet, continuing the trend from 51% to 61% non-human traffic observed year over year.
speaker: Sean Gourley
why: Bots did come to dominate internet traffic, but the claim is unadjudicable without fixing a measurement standard — the Incapsula figures the speaker cited already showed majority-bot traffic at the time he spoke, whereas Cloudflare (which fronts a large share of the web) reported the human/bot crossover only in the first half of 2026.
timing: Depends entirely on the measurement source: Incapsula already reported 61% bot traffic in 2013, while Cloudflare only recorded bots passing humans in H1 2026.

claim: Bot and agent traffic will continue growing exponentially relative to human traffic, reaching roughly a thousand times more bot traffic than human traffic within five years.
speaker: Matthew Prince

claim: For roughly the next two years, the internet will experience a weekly cadence of severe, log4j-scale security vulnerabilities as AI models become extremely proficient at discovering exploits, before software quality dramatically improves once organizations widely adopt AI-based code and configuration review agents.
speaker: Matthew Prince

claim: Nearly every company will go through a workforce-cutting reorganization similar to Cloudflare's within the next 6 to 12 months, as AI tools let managers oversee more direct reports and eliminate the need for as many middle-management and 'measuring' roles.
speaker: Matthew Prince

claim: A new industry/product category is starting to emerge specifically around clustering and analyzing the questions chatbots fail to answer.
speaker: Mike Murchison
why: Analysing unanswered and failed conversations did become a distinct product category — conversation-mining and coverage-gap analytics shipped in Ada, Intercom and Zendesk, and the pattern generalised into the LLM observability and evaluation tooling that followed.

claim: Customer service is converging with the broader customer experience function, pulling service, sales, and marketing closer together.
speaker: Mike Murchison
why: Service, sales and marketing did converge under unified customer-experience platforms — Zendesk, Intercom and Salesforce Service Cloud all repositioned around end-to-end CX rather than ticket handling alone.

claim: As synthetic text, image, and video generation becomes cheap and increasingly indistinguishable from reality, and as this capability is weaponized at scale (state-actor information operations, viral misinformation diffusion), the problem will intensify significantly over the coming 12 to 24 months, making ground-truth verification systems essential.
speaker: Sean Gourley
why: Synthetic media did become cheap and weaponised within the window — deepfake operations and AI-generated influence content proliferated around the 2020 US election, and provenance infrastructure (C2PA, launched 2021) emerged as the ground-truth response predicted.

claim: In the near-to-medium term, AI/ML commercialization in industry will likely remain organized vertical-by-vertical (specialized products per domain) before more convergence toward general-purpose systems happens.
speaker: David Luan
why: The sequencing call was right — AI commercialisation stayed vertical-by-vertical through roughly 2015-2022 (separate vision, speech and NLP products per domain) before foundation models delivered the general-purpose convergence the claim placed later.

claim: Big data will become a new foundation for economic growth and a major competitive differentiator for companies over the next decade.
speaker: Ron Bodkin
why: Over the stated decade data did become a foundational economic input and a genuine competitive differentiator, culminating in an AI buildout whose capital expenditure became macroeconomically significant by the mid-2020s.

claim: New Hadoop/big-data deployments will increasingly start cloud-first rather than on-premises, the way developing countries skipped landline infrastructure and went straight to mobile phones.
speaker: Ashish Thusoo
why: New big-data deployments did go cloud-first and skipped the on-premise generation entirely, exactly as the leapfrog analogy predicted — EMR, Databricks and cloud warehouses became the default starting point while on-premise Hadoop clusters became legacy.

claim: The scale at which on-premises infrastructure becomes more cost-effective than cloud will keep moving further out as cloud economies of scale and competition (Amazon, Google, Azure) continue driving down compute and storage prices.
speaker: Ashish Thusoo
why: Cloud prices did keep falling and the crossover point moved out for most workloads, but the claim ran into a visible counter-trend after 2022 as high-volume companies repatriated workloads on cost grounds, with 37signals publicly documenting multi-million-dollar savings from leaving AWS.

claim: The future of data pipeline creation is conversational: users will prompt an AI to create a pipeline, review a generated draft (e.g., a YAML specification), test it, and publish it via GitOps, replacing today's manual configuration workflows, with a chat-based interface replacing Estuary's current CLI-based Claude Skills workflow within about two months.
why: The two-month product commitment concerns an unreleased internal roadmap item at a private company; Estuary's shipping status for a chat-based pipeline builder is not publicly documented, so the specific claim cannot be checked.

claim: Coding literacy is quickly becoming a non-optional life skill, especially among young people, expanding the pool of STEM professionals who want to work directly with code and data.
speaker: John Fawcett
why: The STEM-pipeline limb held — CS enrolment and the developer population grew substantially through the decade — but coding literacy did not become a non-optional life skill, and LLM code generation has since cut the other way by reducing the need for universal fluency.

claim: Open-sourcing Quantopian's backtester (zipline) will let it become the industry-standard tool for backtesting trading algorithms, benefiting Quantopian competitively even though it gave away core IP.
speaker: John Fawcett
why: Zipline did become a widely used open-source backtester as predicted, but the competitive-benefit limb failed decisively — Quantopian shut down in 2020 and handed zipline to the community, so the open-sourcing did not secure the company's position.

claim: Mobile data volume could grow roughly 90,000-fold over the next 20 years if it continues compounding at the same rate observed over the prior decade (a 300x increase).
speaker: Azeem Azhar

claim: Within the next few years, more AI agents will be surfing the web than humans, which will substantially reshape how the web is monetized, particularly for ad-dependent business models.
speaker: Richard Socher

claim: Scaling horizontally on commodity hardware, now enabled by the cloud, will be a transformative change across this decade.
speaker: Eric Frenkiel
why: Horizontal scale-out on commodity cloud hardware did define the decade's architecture — it became the default assumption behind Kubernetes, cloud data warehouses and distributed SQL, displacing scale-up appliances.

claim: Companies that adopt real-time analytics (rather than tolerating 'big data is slow') will move faster and gain lasting competitive advantage in the marketplace.
speaker: Eric Frenkiel
why: Real-time analytics did become a large and valuable category (Kafka/Confluent, ClickHouse, Druid), but the stronger claim of lasting competitive advantage for adopters is not evidenced — latency became a commodity capability rather than a durable moat.

claim: Within five years, alternative lending will see many more new entrants succeeding in higher-loss-rate segments banks are regulatorily discouraged from serving, with banks increasingly partnering with (rather than competing against) these platforms to originate loans faster or reach populations they can't serve directly.
why: Both limbs held within five years — alternative lenders expanded into thinner-file and higher-loss segments, and bank partnership rather than pure competition became the dominant model, exemplified by Goldman Sachs originating the Apple Card and banks white-labelling fintech origination.

claim: A top-10 global financial institution will emerge that is not today thought of as a bank but as an internet/non-bank technology company (candidates named include Alibaba, Tencent, Facebook, or Google), given how quickly Alipay amassed assets through mobile-native financial products.
why: Ant Group did reach a scale that would have placed it among the largest financial institutions globally and was set for a record IPO, but Chinese regulators halted that listing in November 2020 and forced a restructuring, so the predicted arrival of a top-10 non-bank financial institution was blocked rather than realised.

claim: Some Ada customers will reach 100% automated resolution of customer service conversations within the next two years.
speaker: Mike Murchison
why: Whether specific Ada customers hit 100% automated resolution is a private per-account metric; Ada markets high automated-resolution rates but publishes no verified account reaching the full 100% threshold claimed.

claim: The next scale of big data infrastructure will require thousands of distributed clusters doing edge processing everywhere — inside drones, UAVs, and other autonomous devices.
speaker: M.C. Srivas
