why: Edge inference did become real (on-device vision, autonomous platforms, Jetson-class hardware), but the predicted architecture of thousands of distributed processing clusters did not materialise — compute concentrated dramatically in centralised GPU data centres instead, and MapR itself was distress-sold to HPE in 2019.

claim: Someone will push to revamp the 'dump everything in a data lake and let an LLM figure it out' approach in 2025, but this won't actually work, which is why SQL and data modeling will remain necessary.
speaker: Ben Rogojan
why: Both limbs held in 2025 — vendors did push text-to-SQL and 'point an LLM at the lake' approaches, and the year's practitioner consensus was that semantic layers and disciplined modelling remained necessary, which is precisely why semantic-layer tooling became a focus of the dbt-Fivetran combination.

claim: In 2025, AI initiatives will start moving from press-release-driven announcements to real production deployments, hopefully extending beyond customer service into other use cases companies have quietly been building toward.
speaker: Ben Rogojan
why: 2025 did mark the shift from announcement to deployment, and it did extend past customer service — coding agents in particular moved into genuine production use across engineering organisations that year.

claim: 2025 will see the emergence of more vertical-specific data solutions, such as tools standardizing healthcare claims data, since generic data infrastructure tools extract data well but don't by themselves translate into business value.
speaker: Ben Rogojan
why: Vertical data and AI products did proliferate in 2025, including in the healthcare-claims example named — vertical AI became one of the year's dominant venture theses as generic infrastructure proved insufficient on its own.

claim: Within the next two to three years, everyone doing data science will be using a cloud-based data science productivity platform, since it will be so much better than the status quo.
speaker: Tristan Zajonc
why: By 2016-2017 local development in Jupyter/RStudio on laptops remained overwhelmingly the norm, and Sense itself was acquired by Cloudera in 2016 and wound down; universal adoption of cloud data-science platforms had not happened by the stated deadline and still has not.
timing: Cloud data-science platforms did become mainstream, but nearer 2020-2023 (SageMaker, Databricks, Colab) than the stated 2016-2017, and 'everyone' never held.

claim: Probabilistic programming will emerge as a major unifying approach to statistical modeling over the next few years, letting practitioners describe a domain via simulation rather than hand-picking from a grab-bag of statistical tricks.
speaker: Tristan Zajonc
why: Probabilistic programming did not become a major unifying approach — Stan, PyMC and Pyro remain respected but specialist tools, and the unifying paradigm that actually arrived was deep learning and then foundation models, not simulation-based model specification.

claim: Competition in the big-data infrastructure space will shift from raw scale (which Hadoop has already solved) to speed — delivering interactive, 'human time' analytics rather than batch processing.
speaker: Michael Driscoll
why: The axis of competition did shift from scale to interactive speed exactly as described — Impala, Presto, Druid, ClickHouse and BigQuery all competed on sub-second query latency rather than raw batch capacity.

claim: Most data related to human activity will move from disk-backed storage to in-memory databases within a couple of years, as memory costs follow the same exponential decline as compute and bandwidth.
speaker: Michael Driscoll
why: Most human-activity data did not move to in-memory databases by ~2014 or since; the dominant destination became cheap disk/object storage (S3-style data lakes) with in-memory used as a selective hot tier, and RAM cost per GB did not fall on the exponential curve the claim assumed.

claim: AWS will cross $1 billion in annual revenue within the year of this talk, following 80% year-over-year growth, cementing cloud computing as the default platform for enterprise software.
speaker: Michael Driscoll
why: AWS did cross $1B in annual revenue in 2012 — R.W. Baird estimated ~$1.5B for the year and Morgan Stanley ~$2.2B (Amazon did not break AWS out until 2015). The framing that cloud would become the default enterprise platform also held.

claim: Farm-sensor irrigation algorithms that farmers currently just consult will eventually be piped directly into irrigation systems to automate watering decisions.
speaker: Shivon Zilis
why: Closed-loop automated irrigation does exist commercially (Lindsay FieldNET, Valley, Netafim controllers acting on sensor data), but it remained a minority of irrigated acreage rather than the general replacement of advisory systems the claim envisaged.

claim: Within five years, ordinary professionals will have their own 'army of bots' providing the kind of support staff (schedulers, analysts, editors) that today only CEOs get.
speaker: Shivon Zilis
why: Nothing resembling an 'army of bots' existed for ordinary professionals by 2021, but the capability did arrive later with LLM assistants and multi-agent tooling, making this right in substance and roughly three to five years late.
timing: Personal agent fleets became real around 2024-2026 rather than by the stated 2021.

claim: The city's embedded data-integration infrastructure and practices will persist across mayoral administrations, even if political enthusiasm for data-driven government varies, because reversing it would require someone to actively throw away built-up capability.
speaker: Michael Flowers
why: NYC's analytics capability did survive the Bloomberg-to-de Blasio-to-Adams transitions — the Mayor's Office of Data Analytics and the Open Data Law persisted as institutional infrastructure across all three administrations regardless of shifting political emphasis.

claim: Within a few years, building a technology product without AI will seem as anachronistic as opening a retail shop without any software does today, making AI-driven development ('software 2.0') the norm rather than the exception.
speaker: Clement Delangue

claim: Modalities beyond text, especially audio, video, biology, and chemistry, are the domains that will change the world over the next few years the same way NLP already has in the past.
speaker: Clement Delangue

claim: AI capability progress is not slowing down and shows no visible endpoint for the current line of compounding research improvements to keep driving progress, at least through the next year.
speaker: Sebastian Borgeaud

claim: Retrieval-based research (the original thesis behind Retro, giving models the ability to look up information rather than store all knowledge in parameters) was not yet viable for a leading model but is likely to become viable again for a model like Gemini within the next few years, as post-training and RL scaling mature.
speaker: Sebastian Borgeaud

claim: Cloud adoption's decade-long lag between initial platform growth and massive later-decade wealth creation (as happened with Microsoft and Oracle in the client-server era) will compress into a much shorter roughly 5-to-7-year window this time around.
speaker: Bob Muglia
why: The compression happened as predicted — Snowflake's own 2020 IPO was the largest software listing ever, and the cloud-data wealth creation arrived within roughly five years of the call rather than on the decade-long client-server lag.

claim: Ten years out, big data infrastructure will have moved to the cloud as the clear direction, even though attitudes (e.g. at companies like Bloomberg) have historically resisted this and regulated industries still face a long, socially/regulatorily driven transition.
speaker: Raymie Stata

claim: A large amount of mission-critical data processing, including log/security analytics, will inevitably move to the cloud, with cloud infrastructure adoption set to 'explode' as more companies recognize what's already happening.
speaker: Vance Loiselle
why: Mission-critical log and security analytics did move to cloud SaaS decisively — Datadog, Splunk Cloud and Snowflake-backed security data lakes became standard, and Cisco's $28B acquisition of Splunk in 2024 capped the transition.

claim: Citing an industry study, the volume of unstructured data generated annually will reach roughly 20 million petabytes within two years — about 1,000x what it was five years earlier.
speaker: Vance Loiselle
why: Roughly 20 million petabytes equals 20 zettabytes, which global data creation did not reach by 2016 — IDC put the datasphere near 16ZB that year and 64ZB only by 2020 — so the cited study's two-year figure was optimistic, though the order of magnitude proved directionally sound within a few more years.

claim: The big data market will take roughly 15 years to reach the maturity level traditional BI/relational-database tooling reached — about twice as fast as that earlier market took, because it can build on prior lessons.
speaker: Todd Papaioannou

claim: Over the next 5-7 years, the big data market will produce a wave of new analytic applications as current infrastructure and developer-tooling gaps get filled in.
speaker: Todd Papaioannou
why: The predicted application wave did arrive on schedule — by 2017-2019 the tooling gaps were filled enough to produce a generation of analytic applications (Looker, Amplitude, Mode, Sisu) built atop maturing cloud data infrastructure.

claim: Mobile devices will proliferate to the point that nearly everyone has one, while relatively few people will have traditional computers.
speaker: Todd Papaioannou
why: Mobile did reach near-universal penetration while PC ownership stayed far lower and flat — global smartphone subscriptions passed the multi-billion mark and mobile became the majority of web traffic, exactly the asymmetry described.

claim: The data industry will undergo a fundamental paradigm shift from 'schema at write time' to 'schema at read time' — though a meaningful cohort of traditional data practitioners won't adapt to it.
speaker: Todd Papaioannou
why: Both limbs held — schema-on-read became the default via data lakes and lakehouse table formats, and the predicted practitioner split was visible in the long-running resistance from traditional data-warehouse teams that only partially reconciled through the dbt-led modelling revival.

claim: Fortune 1000 companies are increasingly gravitating toward cloud adoption via VPC environments they control (rather than plain AWS), and this shift is effectively unstoppable.
speaker: Nick Elprin
why: Customer-controlled VPC deployment did become the standard enterprise pattern — bring-your-own-cloud and private-link architectures are now offered by Databricks, Snowflake and most enterprise data vendors precisely to satisfy Fortune 1000 control requirements.

claim: Analytics engineering will meaningfully improve over the next two years as AI accelerates tasks like code authoring, testing, and documentation, though what happens beyond that horizon is too uncertain to predict.
speaker: Tristan Handy
why: Analytics engineering did improve materially over the two-year window as AI took on SQL authoring, testing and documentation — dbt shipped AI-assisted development and the Fusion engine, and LLM code assistance became routine in analytics workflows.

claim: Apple will continue to build more beautiful, premium products than Amazon, while Amazon's products will continue to be cheaper — because these differences are integral to each company's distinct culture and strategy, not something either could casually borrow from the other.
speaker: Ben Horowitz
why: The positioning held through the period — Apple continued to occupy the premium tier while Amazon's Echo, Fire and Kindle lines stayed price-led, with neither company crossing into the other's strategy as the cultural argument predicted.

claim: Within three years, every company in the world will use NLP, and companies that don't will be at a systemic disadvantage in understanding their users, customers, and employees.
speaker: Clement Delangue
why: By the 2023 deadline NLP was widespread but far from universal; the claim effectively came true only after ChatGPT drove language models into general enterprise use, and 'every company in the world' remains an overstatement even now.
timing: Near-universal language-model use arrived around 2024-2025, roughly a year or two past the stated three-year window.

claim: Rather than one platform (Snowflake or Databricks) consolidating the whole data/AI stack, the near-term future will be a 'polyglot persistence' of many vendors and configurations.
why: No single platform consolidated the stack in the near term — enterprises continued running heterogeneous combinations of Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, DuckDB and specialised engines, and the open table-format war reinforced rather than ended that plurality.

claim: Crowdsourced, mobile-collected data exhaust (in the mold of Foursquare check-ins recreating transit networks) will become a primary source of macroeconomic data, replacing or supplementing today's slow official statistics collection.
speaker: Joe Reisinger
why: Alternative and crowdsourced data did become an established supplement to official statistics (Premise itself pivoted successfully to government and development contracts), but it supplemented rather than replaced official collection, and national statistical agencies remain the primary macroeconomic source.

claim: The data science/AI industry is only about 20-25% of the way through its enterprise adoption cycle: early-adopter organizations from three to four years earlier already run mature 50-200 person data teams delivering business-critical results, while most other organizations are just starting and will follow their lead over the next several years.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: The directional claim that most organisations were early and would follow the leaders proved right, but '20-25% of the way through' has no measurable denominator — the enterprise adoption cycle has no defined endpoint, so the specific figure cannot be graded.

claim: Global manufacturing broadly (beyond high-tech manufacturing like aerospace and microchips, which is adopting fastest due to mature sensor infrastructure) will catch up in data-driven predictive maintenance and optimization within roughly the next 10 years, gated by how long it takes each subsector to rebuild factories with the sensor data needed.
speaker: Florian Douetteau

claim: Machine learning workflows will become increasingly automated over the next few years, though along a controllable gradient (like a camera's auto versus manual modes) rather than a single one-size-fits-all level of automation, so expert users retain the ability to intervene while novice users can rely on full auto-ML.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: ML tooling did converge on exactly the graduated-control model described — AutoML products from Google, DataRobot and H2O, and later LLM tooling, all ship automatic defaults with expert override rather than a single fixed automation level.

claim: Extrapolating current benchmark trends, models will be able to work autonomously for a full day's worth of tasks by around 2026, at least one model will match industry experts across many occupations by late 2026, and models will frequently outperform experts on many tasks by 2027.
speaker: Julian Schrittwieser

claim: An AI system will likely make a scientific discovery significant enough for near-unanimous agreement that it deserves a Nobel Prize sometime around 2027-2028, following the same trajectory shown by AlphaFold's Nobel-winning impact.
speaker: Julian Schrittwieser

claim: By the end of 2025 to 2026, two-thirds of SDR (sales development rep) positions will no longer exist, per a CRM company CEO's estimate, as AI automates outbound sales development.
speaker: Tomasz Tunguz

claim: Within 18 to 24 months, the average software company should see gross margins improve by two to five percentage points as AI-driven efficiency gains outweigh the added inference costs of generative AI features.
speaker: Tomasz Tunguz
why: No broad two-to-five-point gross-margin improvement appeared in software company reporting over the window; the dominant narrative through 2025-26 ran the other way, with inference costs pressuring margins at AI-heavy software companies, though attribution at the sector average is genuinely hard to isolate.

claim: Software development is shifting toward developers avoiding infrastructure management entirely, provisioning managed services (databases, and now log/metrics tools like Splunk Storm) instead of standing up and operating their own hardware.
speaker: Stephen Sorkin
why: Developers did move decisively to managed services and away from operating their own infrastructure — RDS, managed Kubernetes, serverless and observability SaaS became the default, and the term 'serverless' entered general use shortly after.

claim: Within five to ten years, 'big data' as a distinct category will disappear, and companies that simply incorporate big data capabilities into their applications will win against those that don't, the same way Google and Facebook won by having the data.
speaker: Mike Dauber
why: 'Big data' did fade as a distinct product category within the stated 5-10 year window — Gartner retired it from its hype cycle and vendors repositioned around cloud data platforms and AI — and the winners were companies embedding data capability into applications rather than selling the category itself.

claim: It would take a bold, heterodox claim to argue that 75% of people won't be using AI chatbots daily within less than seven years of ChatGPT's November 2022 launch, following a faster-than-iPhone adoption trajectory.
speaker: Azeem Azhar

claim: Self-driving cars and mainstream VR/AR adoption will likely arrive somewhere between 2 and 10 years from now, following the pattern of prior technology cycles that run in roughly 10-to-15-year waves.
speaker: Chris Dixon

claim: New computing platforms (IoT, wearables, drones, VR/AR, self-driving cars) will be the next major technology mega-trend, following the pattern of social, mobile, and cloud over the prior decade.
speaker: Chris Dixon
why: None of the named platforms became the next mega-trend — VR/AR stalled badly (Meta's Reality Labs lost tens of billions), self-driving stayed limited and drones and wearables remained niche, while the actual successor wave was generative AI, which the list did not include.

claim: Within five years, it will be considered a no-brainer that security must be attached to observability, since most vulnerabilities are introduced and fixed by the same development and operations teams already using observability tools.
speaker: Olivier Pomel

claim: Companies will start treating their proprietary data less possessively and more open to shared/pooled model training within the next 5 to 10 years, though probably not within the next year.
speaker: Mark Johnson

claim: It's a near certainty Amazon's AWS business will reach $100 billion in revenue at around 20% operating margins and roughly 90% market share, making it the single biggest threat facing open source business models.
speaker: Peter Fenton
why: AWS did reach a $100B annual revenue run rate (2024) at operating margins near or above the predicted 20%, but the 90% market share limb was badly wrong — AWS held roughly 30% of cloud infrastructure by then, with Azure and Google Cloud taking most of the rest.
timing: The $100B revenue mark arrived in 2024, roughly eight years after the claim.

claim: As still-overvalued private companies eventually can't avoid repricing and run out of runway, corporate M&A activity, which hasn't really started yet, is going to pick up and won't be pleasant for founders holding out for old valuations.
speaker: Peter Fenton
why: The predicted painful repricing did eventually occur — the 2022-23 downturn brought widespread down rounds, shutdowns and distressed acquisitions — but not on the near-term timeline implied in 2016, since capital instead stayed abundant for another five years.
timing: The repricing and shakeout arrived in 2022-2023, roughly six years after the call rather than imminently.

claim: Fragmented modern data stack categories, semantic layers, data catalogs, ETL tools, will consolidate into a much smaller number of categories within about three years.
speaker: Mike Palmer

claim: Social data usage across businesses is still at roughly 1% of its eventual scale and will go on to change all business operations, extending well beyond social media monitoring into areas like supply chain management and retail.
speaker: Chris Moody
why: Social data did extend beyond monitoring into supply chain and retail signals, but its trajectory was cut short rather than growing 100x — platform API restrictions after Cambridge Analytica and Twitter's 2023 API repricing shut down much of the ecosystem Gnip pioneered.

claim: Social data will increasingly feed into the existing $40 billion business intelligence industry (traditional data warehouses and BI platforms like Oracle and IBM), rather than remaining a standalone category.
speaker: Chris Moody
why: The directional limb held — social data became a connector into mainstream BI and warehouse pipelines rather than a standalone category — but the 'increasingly' magnitude failed, as platform API lockdowns after Cambridge Analytica and Twitter's 2023 repricing shrank the addressable social-data supply rather than growing it.

claim: Within the next 5-10 years, the industry will move toward networks of smart, connected devices with embedded, self-retraining predictive models, extending big data beyond insight generation toward automating decisions.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: The decision-automation limb held — ML did move from insight to automated action across pricing, fraud and logistics — but the embedded self-retraining device-network limb did not, as continuous on-device retraining stayed rare and inference concentrated centrally.

claim: Over the next 5 years, data science innovation will spread beyond a handful of digital giants to many more companies.
speaker: Florian Douetteau
why: Data science did diffuse well beyond the digital giants within five years — cloud ML platforms, open-source frameworks and managed AutoML put capability within reach of mid-market and traditional enterprises by 2021.

claim: By 2025, computer chips will be as fast as the human brain, per Ray Kurzweil's accelerating-growth projections.
speaker: Stefan Groschupf
why: Whether this resolved by 2025 depends entirely on the brain-equivalence figure chosen: exascale supercomputers (Frontier, >10^18 FLOPS) exceed common estimates of brain compute, while no single chip does, and the underlying Kurzweil framing gives no operational definition. Genuinely contested.

claim: In a short period of time, deep learning will be phenomenal and ubiquitous, reducing the value of traditional feature-engineering-focused data science careers.
speaker: Stefan Groschupf
why: The ubiquity limb held emphatically and the devaluation-of-feature-engineering limb held for perception tasks, but classical feature work remained central to tabular and business ML throughout, where gradient boosting still outperforms deep nets.
timing: Deep learning did become ubiquitous, but over roughly 5-8 years rather than 'a short period of time'.

claim: Since San Francisco/Bay Area adoption of Slack was already near saturation, most of Slack's future growth would happen in other parts of the world.
speaker: Noah Weiss
why: Slack's growth after 2016 did come overwhelmingly from outside the saturated Bay Area — by its 2019 direct listing the company reported customers in over 150 countries with roughly a third of revenue international.

claim: The next five years will be a hallmark period for CTOs, forcing major decisions across talent strategy, architecture, team structure, governance, and security as AI reshapes how engineering organizations operate.
Multi-billion-dollar companies will emerge that figure out how to efficiently measure DNA variants, deliver that information to patients, and build feedback loops from patient outcomes.
speaker: Mark Kaganovich
why: Multi-billion-dollar genomics companies did emerge on variant measurement and delivery (Illumina, Tempus, Guardant), but the patient-outcome feedback-loop limb largely failed — 23andMe collapsed into bankruptcy in 2025, showing the consumer-genomics-to-outcomes loop did not become a durable business.

claim: If the data infrastructure problem isn't solved, precision medicine will look back on itself in 10 years as having resembled the past more than the future.
speaker: Mark Kaganovich
why: Genomic data infrastructure improved substantially over the decade, yet precision medicine remains concentrated in oncology and rare disease rather than generalised; whether that counts as 'resembling the past more than the future' depends on an unstated benchmark, and the claim's conditional framing makes it hard to fail.

claim: Large data-licensing deals like 23andMe's, where companies monetize consented genomic and clinical datasets by selling access to pharma and other consumers of the data, are going to happen more and more often.
speaker: Mark Kaganovich
why: Genomic data-licensing deals did proliferate — 23andMe's $300M GSK partnership in 2018 was followed by comparable arrangements from Regeneron, deCODE and health systems monetising consented clinical and genomic cohorts.

claim: Chatbots and conversational-interface products will largely fail outside China, because they were driven by hype ('a hammer looking for a nail') rather than genuine consumer demand, and will eventually get folded into larger platforms that meet more basic human needs, the way earlier content-discovery/personalization startups were absorbed into Facebook, Twitter, and LinkedIn.
speaker: Bradford Cross
why: The 2016-17 chatbot cohort did largely fail as predicted (Facebook M shut down in 2018, the bot-platform wave collapsed), but the underlying reasoning — that people don't want conversational interfaces — was decisively refuted by ChatGPT five years later, making this right on the near-term call and wrong on the mechanism.

claim: Machine-learning-as-a-service cloud APIs from major providers (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, IBM) will fail commercially a second time, since teams with real ML talent will keep replicating commodity capabilities in-house cheaply once usage volume makes the API's economics unfavorable.
speaker: Bradford Cross
why: Cloud ML APIs did not fail a second time — they became one of the largest revenue lines in software, with Azure OpenAI, Bedrock and Vertex AI driving hyperscaler growth, and the in-house-replication economics the claim relied on were overwhelmed by frontier models nobody could cheaply reproduce.

claim: Oncology will likely see substantial machine learning-driven innovation over the next 20 years because well-defined, accessible datasets already exist in that domain.
speaker: Auren Hoffman

claim: Nutrition science will likely see little progress over the next 20 years (people will still be following fad diets), because collecting comprehensive data linking everything a person eats to outcomes that may not appear for decades is an extremely difficult data collection problem.
speaker: Auren Hoffman

claim: Within the next five years, privacy-preserving techniques (running algorithms against sensitive datasets like hospital or IRS records without directly exposing the underlying data) will likely become available to solve today's data-access privacy barriers.
speaker: Auren Hoffman
why: The techniques did become available within five years — differential privacy shipped in the 2020 US Census, and federated learning and confidential computing reached production — but they did not solve the data-access barrier, which remains primarily legal and institutional rather than technical.

claim: Automated machine learning represents a major shift in how people will consume machine learning and big data technology going forward, expanding access beyond a limited pool of trained data scientists.
speaker: Stephen Purpura
why: AutoML did materially widen access to machine learning — Google AutoML, DataRobot, H2O and later LLM-based tooling let analysts and domain experts build models without formal data science training, exactly the consumption shift described.

claim: The percentage of Hadoop cluster compute cycles spent on MapReduce specifically will asymptotically approach zero, not because MapReduce usage will shrink but because so much other processing (Spark, Impala, etc.) will be added on top.
speaker: Mike Olson
why: The outcome limb held — MapReduce's share of cycles did fall toward zero — but the explicitly stated mechanism failed: Olson said this would happen 'not because MapReduce usage will shrink', and MapReduce usage did shrink absolutely as workloads migrated to Spark and Hadoop clusters themselves contracted into the Cloudera-Hortonworks merger.

claim: As with the relational database market (where roughly $30B/year in platform spending was dwarfed by about $70B/year in services and applications on top), the lion's share of money spent in the big data market will go to applications built on the platform, not to the platform itself.
speaker: Mike Olson
why: Value did concentrate above the platform layer — the open-source infrastructure itself was largely commoditised while applications and managed services captured the spend, a pattern confirmed by Cloudera's own decline to a $5.3B take-private in 2021 against the scale of application-layer data businesses.

claim: Virtually every vertical market will become significantly big-data-driven, extending well beyond the current early-adopter industries (financial services, retail, telco).
speaker: Mike Olson
why: Data-driven operation did spread across essentially all verticals over the following decade — manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, healthcare and the public sector all built substantial data and ML functions well beyond the 2014 early-adopter set.

claim: Over roughly the next six months, AI will produce more math and science breakthroughs of the kind seen with the unit distance problem, and the same capabilities will increasingly be turned on AI research itself, making models progressively more central to AI's own development, though without one single sharp transition to full self-improvement.
speaker: Dan Roberts

claim: A joking extrapolation (doubling autonomous 'thinking time' from current benchmarks) projected roughly nine years to reach a model that can autonomously think for as long as Einstein spent discovering general relativity, but this projection will almost certainly break down before then, since future models will be so much more powerful that letting a system 'think' for a fixed multi-year duration will no longer make sense as a benchmark.
speaker: Dan Roberts
horizon: 9 years (self-described as likely to break down earlier)

claim: 5G and edge computing won't meaningfully change observability's real-time requirements, since Datadog already operates on a few-seconds round trip — the latency-sensitive problems 5G/edge actually affect (like video) are a different part of the stack.
speaker: Olivier Pomel
why: The skeptical call held — 5G and edge did not reshape observability requirements, Datadog's architecture and market position were unaffected, and the company continued compounding growth without an edge-driven redesign.

claim: AI video and AI voice will look fundamentally different from today's within five years, unlocking new formats (analogous to how drum machines and synthesizers didn't replace drummers/pianists but created new music genres like electronica and techno) rather than simply replacing existing camera-shot video.
speaker: Victor Riparbelli

claim: The shift of Fortune 1000 companies toward cloud adoption for big data, having moved from all-or-nothing stances to hybrid deployments over the prior five years, is accelerating and will keep accelerating.
speaker: Ashish Thusoo
why: Fortune 1000 cloud adoption for data workloads did keep accelerating after 2016, with hybrid becoming the standard posture and cloud data platform revenue compounding at high rates through the following decade.

claim: Generative AI's impact will not fade after one hype cycle; the core technology has decades of transformative effect still ahead of it across every industry, regardless of short-term market swings.
speaker: Morgan McGuire

claim: The central challenge facing generative AI over the next two to three years will be giving creators fine-grained, iterative control over generative models, moving beyond brittle prompt engineering toward direct visual/compositional input.
speaker: Morgan McGuire

claim: 2024's central enterprise AI question is whether generative AI spending shifts from innovation budgets (proof-of-concept money) into real operational budgets, as companies identify concrete, durable use cases.
why: This framing of 2024's central question proved accurate — the innovation-budget-to-operational-budget transition was exactly the axis enterprise AI was debated on that year, and Gartner's proof-of-concept abandonment finding shows it was genuinely unresolved rather than settled.

claim: Within three to five years, people will use conversational AI interfaces rather than search engines for high-value commercial queries like shopping for auto insurance, with the agent querying multiple providers and returning summarized options.
speaker: Sridhar Ramaswamy

claim: 2025 will be the year of AI agents, and the year generative AI graduates from being an assistant to functioning as a genuine co-worker.
speaker: Daniel
why: The agent limb held — 2025 was decisively the year agents moved into production, especially in coding — but the 'genuine co-worker' limb overshot, since agents remained closely supervised tools requiring human review rather than autonomous colleagues.

claim: OLAP and OLTP database technologies are converging toward more general-purpose systems, a trend playing out across the industry and not unique to ClickHouse.
speaker: Aaron Katz
why: OLTP/OLAP convergence became a real industry trend — Postgres gained columnar and analytical extensions, SingleStore and TiDB pushed HTAP, and Snowflake added transactional tables (Unistore), confirming the pattern was general rather than ClickHouse-specific.

claim: Data center NIMBYism, driven by energy, water, and geopolitical concerns, will become too large an issue for voters to ignore and will take precedence in major 2026 political campaigns.
speaker: Nathan Benaich

claim: A formal language and paradigm for transforming and operating on streaming data in real time (analogous to what SQL became for relational data) doesn't exist yet but will need to be developed, benefiting the whole data ecosystem once it does.
speaker: Kirill Sheynkman
why: Streaming SQL did emerge as the missing formalism and benefited the ecosystem broadly — Flink SQL, ksqlDB and Materialize established SQL-over-streams as the standard paradigm, and the community codified streaming semantics through the Dataflow model.

claim: The machine-to-machine automated reaction pattern already common in algorithmic trading will extend to other real-time data domains, including social media, with intelligent systems reacting to signals rather than relying on humans watching dashboards.
speaker: Kirill Sheynkman
why: Automated machine-to-machine reaction did spread far beyond trading — real-time fraud scoring, programmatic ad bidding, dynamic pricing and automated content moderation all replaced humans watching dashboards, exactly as the algorithmic-trading analogy predicted.

claim: Startups whose business model is just 'we generate or hold lots of data and will monetize it' will largely fail, because selling raw data directly is a difficult business.
speaker: Kirill Sheynkman
why: Pure data-monetisation startups did largely fail — the raw-data-brokerage model proved commercially weak and legally exposed, with privacy regulation and platform API lockdowns (Twitter, Facebook) removing the supply that such businesses depended on.

claim: The 'big data' hype will only be validated if, within 5-10 years, companies widely have C-level executives who own the data/science function and use it to drive core business decisions, rather than data merely being about cheaper storage and processing.
speaker: Vijay Subramanian
why: The CDO-appointment limb was met — the role became standard across the Fortune 1000 within the window — but the second limb, executives actually using it to drive core business decisions, was not: successive industry surveys through the period reported a minority of firms describing themselves as data-driven, alongside notably short CDO tenures.

claim: Internet payments infrastructure (mobile payments, micropayments, merchant processing) will end up running on Bitcoin's blockchain rather than today's patched-together bank and credit-card rails.
speaker: Fred Wilson
why: Thirteen years on, mainstream internet payments still run on card networks and bank rails (Visa/Mastercard/ACH plus Stripe-style processors); Bitcoin's blockchain did not become the settlement layer for mobile payments, micropayments, or merchant processing, and what crypto payment volume exists has migrated to stablecoins on other chains.

claim: New York will maintain a real, lasting expertise advantage in data science, rooted in its decades-long quant-finance culture, as data science gets applied to more industries beyond finance.
speaker: Fred Wilson
why: New York retained a genuine data-science cluster rooted in finance and media, but the decisive AI concentration of the following decade went overwhelmingly to the Bay Area, so whether NY held a 'real, lasting expertise advantage' depends on whether you measure against all other cities or against the actual leader.

claim: Fintech bundling is shifting from geography-based (the old local, all-purpose 'big box bank' relationship) to demographic-based, with companies like Robinhood and Goldman Sachs' Marcus building tailored product suites around specific customer segments and growing via network effects.
speaker: Zach Perret
why: The demographic-bundling thesis broadly held as neobanks and segment-focused fintechs scaled, but one of the two named exemplars failed — Goldman retreated from Marcus consumer banking at significant loss — undercutting the specific evidence offered.

claim: Consumers with relatively simple financial lives will increasingly be able to live an almost fully digital financial life, as more banks launch fully digital sub-brands and banks/fintechs both partner and compete, ultimately benefiting consumers through more choice and lower prices.
speaker: Zach Perret
why: A fully digital financial life did become achievable for consumers with simple needs — digital-only banks scaled, incumbents launched digital sub-brands, and bank-fintech partnership plus competition expanded choice and cut fees as described.

claim: Consumers will soon start being compensated for the value companies extract from their personal data (e.g., a carrier offering free service in exchange for data use), and if companies don't offer that value-sharing voluntarily, government regulation will eventually force it.
speaker: Chris Lynch
why: Neither limb arrived on the stated 'shortly' timeline — no meaningful consumer data-dividend market emerged, and while privacy regulation did expand (GDPR, CCPA), it granted deletion and access rights rather than compelling the value-sharing compensation described.

claim: Current sky-high valuations in the Hadoop/big-data space are unsustainable and will correct painfully, driven by too much venture capital chasing too few genuinely good entrepreneurs and ideas.
speaker: Chris Lynch
why: The Hadoop-era valuation correction was severe and painful exactly as predicted — Hortonworks was forced into a merger with Cloudera in 2019 and the combined company was taken private in 2021 for $5.3B, far below the sector's peak private and public marks.

claim: Within 5 to 10 years, demand for radiologists will grow rather than shrink because medical imaging volume will increase, but every radiologist will be empowered by AI tools across scanning, diagnosis, and reporting.
speaker: Emi Gal

claim: Over the next decade, most innovation in MRI will come from software rather than hardware, since scanner magnet strength has essentially hit its practical ceiling for safe human use.
speaker: Emi Gal

claim: Extrapolating from current energy-per-neuron trends, it would take roughly 50 years for artificial neural systems to reach the scale of the human brain.
speaker: Christopher Nguyen

claim: If brain-machine interfaces are implemented within the next 50 years, humans could become a 'hyper-evolved,' AI-augmented species.
speaker: Christopher Nguyen

claim: The truly great, transformative AI companies of this technology cycle haven't been founded yet — that generation of companies will likely emerge within the next 5-10 years.
speaker: Christopher Nguyen
why: The prediction landed almost exactly — Anthropic (2021), Mistral (2023) and the transformation of OpenAI into a major commercial entity all occurred within the stated 5-10 year window, and these became the cycle's defining AI companies.

claim: 2025 will be the year AI adoption moves past experimentation and prototyping into real production use cases, pushing past the current hype-cycle skepticism, with RAG playing an essential role in making AI production-ready.
speaker: Justin Borgman
why: The production-adoption limb held for 2025, but the RAG-as-essential limb aged poorly within the year as long-context models, agentic search and tool use displaced classical retrieval pipelines as the default pattern.

claim: Flink's contributor community, which roughly doubled the prior year, is expected to keep growing at a similar rate going forward.
speaker: Kostas Tzoumas
why: Flink's community did keep growing and the project became the streaming standard, but not at a sustained doubling rate; data Artisans was sold to Alibaba in 2019 and Flink's expansion thereafter was steady rather than exponential.

claim: Every organization is going to need a dedicated insight platform, as essential as a CRM or HRM tool, so they aren't blindsided by what's happening with their customers, market, and employees.
speaker: Ryan Smith
why: Experience management did become a recognised enterprise software category — Qualtrics itself reached an $8B SAP acquisition and a later $12.5B take-private — but it did not achieve CRM-or-HRM-level universality, remaining a discretionary rather than essential system.

claim: The way organizations buy enterprise software is totally changing, shifting away from top-down executive mandates toward bottom-up adoption driven by internal champions.
speaker: Ryan Smith
why: Bottom-up adoption did displace top-down mandates as the dominant enterprise software motion — product-led growth became the standard playbook, exemplified by Slack, Figma, Datadog and Snowflake entering organisations through practitioners rather than executive procurement.

claim: Big data analytics will shift away from rigid, predefined-model BI toward hypothesis-driven, iterative 'converged analysis' that intelligently combines diverse private and external data sources, becoming the new standard approach.
speaker: Sharmila Mulligan
why: Exploratory, iterative analysis blending internal and external data did become normal practice, but the predicted displacement of modelled BI did not occur — the dbt-led revival re-established disciplined semantic modelling as the standard, and ClearStory itself did not survive as an independent company.

claim: Excel will still be widely used in five years and even in ten years, since enterprise technology adoption lags far behind the pace of AI innovation, even as generative AI replaces many of the underlying tasks people currently use spreadsheets for.
speaker: Eleonor Crespo

claim: Pigment aims to expand well beyond enterprise performance management into adjacent categories over the next five to ten years, ultimately building toward a $100-200 billion company that behaves more like a fully-fledged suite comparable to SAP or Oracle, but with far higher user satisfaction.
speaker: Eleonor Crespo

claim: Backpropagation and current deep learning techniques alone will not be sufficient to reach human-level general learning ability, contrary to optimistic deep learning researchers who believe more data and compute will get there; progress will instead require unifying multiple learning paradigms, and possibly discovering an entirely new sixth paradigm beyond the five that have existed since the 1950s.
speaker: Pedro Domingos
why: Human-level general learning has not been reached, consistent with the claim, and RL post-training did add a paradigm beyond pure backpropagation-on-more-data; but the scaling advocates Domingos criticised produced far more capability than he anticipated, and no 'sixth paradigm' has appeared, so the verdict turns on how much of the gap remains.

claim: AI poses a far greater immediate risk through incompetence (flawed, opaque systems already making consequential decisions about people) than through any near-term superintelligent takeover scenario, and the most important AI safety work is making systems less black-box and more accurate/comprehensible, not preventing hypothetical runaway intelligence.
speaker: Pedro Domingos
why: The near-term harms Domingos prioritised are the ones that materialised and drew regulatory response — opaque automated decisions in hiring, credit and benefits drove the EU AI Act's high-risk provisions and US agency enforcement, while superintelligent takeover remained hypothetical.

claim: There will be new and better data processing technology next year than exists this year, making designing for continuous technological change (rather than a fixed target) essential.
speaker: Mike Tuchen
why: Trivially borne out — 2019 brought materially better data processing technology than 2018 (Delta Lake, Iceberg's rise, Spark 3.0 development), and the pace of change since has vindicated designing for continuous change. Trivially true as stated ('next year will bring better technology than this year') and attached to normative advice; per spec §3.6 this is a candidate for reclassification as unscoreable-by-form rather than a scored correct.

claim: 2025 will be both the year of AI agents, with thousands of agents being built for specific problems, and the year of open models, following DeepSeek's role in setting a new baseline for open-source model quality.
speaker: Lin Qiao
why: Both limbs held for 2025 — agents proliferated across specific problem domains, and open models became genuinely competitive following DeepSeek's R1 release, which reset expectations for open-weight quality.

claim: The majority, if not all, developers in the world will adopt some form of AI pair-programming assistant within the next couple of years.
speaker: Eiso Kant

claim: Within about three years, non-engineers with no software development background will be able to describe a high-level, vague vision for an app and have an AI system ask the right questions to build it.
speaker: Eiso Kant

claim: Having a big-data capability will stop being a competitive advantage and become table stakes — like just-in-time ('zero stock') inventory became to manufacturing — where lacking it means you lose, but having it only puts you at parity with competitors.
speaker: Matt Turck
why: Data capability did become table stakes rather than differentiation — cloud warehouses and ML tooling commoditised the capability so thoroughly that lacking it is a liability while having it confers no particular edge, exactly the just-in-time analogy drawn.

claim: The 'plumbing' layer of the big data ecosystem (infrastructure and tooling companies) will consolidate through acquisition as large companies buy the pieces they need.
speaker: Matt Turck
why: The plumbing layer consolidated heavily through acquisition — Cloudera-Hortonworks, HPE-MapR, Workday-Platfora, Cisco-Splunk, Alibaba-data Artisans and the Fivetran-dbt merger all followed exactly this pattern.

claim: Big data infrastructure tools will become taken for granted and invisible to users, the way social media went from a novel capability to an assumed default in a few years.
speaker: Matt Turck
why: Data infrastructure did become invisible plumbing — serverless warehouses and managed pipelines mean practitioners now query without knowing or caring about the underlying cluster, matching the social-media-becomes-assumed analogy.

claim: A second wave of genuinely new business models, not just better infrastructure, will emerge from big data — enabling things like usage-based pricing (Rolls-Royce's jet engines) and hyper-customized products (3D printing).
speaker: Matt Turck
why: The usage-based-pricing limb held strongly — consumption pricing became standard across cloud and AI software — but the hyper-customised-products limb did not, as 3D printing stayed a prototyping and niche manufacturing technology rather than enabling mass customisation.

claim: The hype around 'big data' will eventually trigger a backlash as people realize challenges like the difficulty of installing Hadoop and the scarcity of data science talent.
speaker: Matt Turck
why: The backlash arrived on cue and for the stated reasons — Gartner moved big data into the trough of disillusionment, and the operational difficulty of Hadoop plus the data-scientist talent shortage were the two most cited causes.

claim: By existing and creating competitive transparency, StellaService will influence businesses broadly to allocate more money toward customer service and experience, even among companies that aren't StellaService clients.
speaker: Jordy Leiser & Dave Miller
why: No study isolates StellaService's spillover effect on non-client customer-service budgets, and the company was absorbed into Deloitte, so the counterfactual industry influence claimed cannot be measured.

claim: Over the next ten years, the internet will reorganize itself around MCP-style integrations, producing widespread cross-pollination between products and novel interfaces that were previously possible in theory but too difficult to build.
speaker: Guillermo Rauch
